law.d: An instrument that binds the reader directly: a statute, a directive as transposed, a regulation, a ratified convention, or a condition attached to a licence. Non-compliance is unlawful, not merely unjustified.

own.d: A requirement issued by the future owner or operator rather than by a state: a utility requirement set, a bid specification. It binds through contract, not through law, and only once a contract adopts it.

reg.d: Guidance a regulator expects to see followed, or an international safety standard a regulator has adopted as its reference. Departure is permitted but must be justified in the safety case, so in practice it behaves as a requirement.

code.d: A design, manufacturing or in-service code written for nuclear items, keyed to a safety class. It binds only through the route that adopts it: a licence condition, a regulatory endorsement, or a contract.

std.d: A consensus standard not written for nuclear duty but applied to nuclear projects, typically to items outside the safety classes or to management processes.

guide.d: Collected operating experience, good practice and method reports from industry bodies and technical organisations. It carries no authority; it carries evidence.

method.d: A computational method or code family used to produce an analysis. It is not a requirement. What matters in a file is its validation basis and its applicability to the plant and the phenomena analysed.

worked.d: Individual documents are named and described. The layer is still incomplete, but a filter result here is a real reading list.

outline.d: The regulator and the families of instruments are named; individual documents are not. Usually because the authoritative text is in the national language and the available translations are unofficial. Treat a result here as a map of where to look, not as a list of what applies.

frame.d: This register carries no national layer at all. What it can tell you is the framework above that jurisdiction: for a member state of the Union, the Euratom directives and the WENRA reference levels; for anywhere else, the IAEA safety standards and the conventions the state has ratified. The national regime is what turns those into obligations, and it is not in this register.

nonjur.d: Consensus standards, scientific recommendations, industry material and calculation methods that belong to no state. They acquire force only where a law, a licence condition or a contract picks them up.

D31: Binds contracting parties to maintain a legislative and regulatory framework for land-based civil power reactors and to report periodically.
It creates obligations for states, not for licensees, and it excludes non-reactor facilities.
D32: Joint Convention on spent fuel and radioactive waste
Binds contracting parties on the safety of spent fuel and radioactive waste management, including national inventories and reporting.
It does not regulate any facility directly.
D33: Treaty obligations on the physical protection of nuclear material in use, storage and transport, extended by the 2005 Amendment to domestic use and sabotage.
Implementation is entirely through national law.
D34: The legal basis for IAEA safeguards: declarations, design information, inspections and complementary access.
Declaration content and timing are set by the agreement with your state, not by the project.
D35: Obliges notification and consultation with neighbouring states for activities likely to have significant transboundary effects.
Whether your project triggers it is a determination made by the competent authority.
D36: Access to information and public participation
Obliges access to environmental information, public participation in decisions and access to justice.
It does not tell you what to publish about a nuclear facility.
D37: The international liability regime: channelling to the operator, minimum amounts, financial security and jurisdiction.
Which convention applies, and at what amount, depends on your state's adherence.
D38: The system of radiological protection: justification, optimisation, dose limits and constraints, and the exposure situations.
ICRP recommends. Only the national transposition binds anyone.
D39: Establishes the EU framework for nuclear installation safety: regulator independence, the safety objective for new installations, periodic safety review, peer review topics.
It is transposed nationally. What binds you is the transposition, not the directive text.
D40: Transposes the radiological protection system into EU law: dose limits, clearance, exemption, emergency and existing exposure situations.
Clearance and exemption values are given in its annexes and are applied through national transposition.
D41: EU spent fuel and radioactive waste directive
Requires a national policy and national programme for spent fuel and waste management, including disposal.
It does not set technical requirements for any facility.
D42: Requires an EIA for projects likely to have significant effects on the environment, and sets the content of the assessment.
The scope of your assessment is set by the competent authority in the scoping step.
D43: Requires assessment of plans and programmes, which is where a national nuclear programme is assessed.
It applies to the programme, not to your project.
D44: Euratom Treaty environmental and investment articles
Article 37 requires general data on radioactive discharges to be submitted to the Commission before authorisation; Articles 41 to 44 require notification of investment projects.
These are procedural obligations with deadlines. They do not review your safety case.
D45: The accountancy, reporting and design-information obligations of operators towards the Commission.
It runs alongside, not instead of, IAEA safeguards.
D46: EU network and information security directive
Cyber security obligations for essential entities, which in most member states includes nuclear operators.
Its relationship to safety I&C security is set nationally and is often contested.
D47: WENRA reference levels and safety objectives
A harmonised European set of reference levels for existing reactors and safety objectives for new designs, widely used as the benchmark in licensing.
WENRA is an association of regulators, not a legislator. Its force comes from national adoption.
D55: Addresses the design and construction of vessels, piping, pumps, valves, supports, core support structures and containments for nuclear service.
The correspondence between the safety classification of an item and the construction rules applied to it is a project decision that has to be justified.
D56: The US rules for in-service inspection and testing of nuclear power plant components.
It presupposes construction to the matching code.
D62: The German safety standard series covering mechanical, civil, electrical, I&C, ventilation and quality aspects, published openly.
The series was written around the German fleet and is maintained on a limited basis.
D63: code requirements for nuclear safety related concrete structures
Addresses the design of safety-related concrete structures on nuclear sites.
It has to be paired with a separate definition of the loads and their combinations, which it does not supply.
D64: Instrumentation and control important to safety: general requirements for systems
The framework standard for nuclear I&C architecture, categorisation and the relation between system and equipment standards.
It is the top of a standard series. The lower standards carry the detail.
D65: software for computer-based systems performing the most safety-significant functions
Addresses how software for the most safety-significant class of nuclear I&C functions is to be developed, verified and justified.
It is one standard in a series; software developed before the project, and the tools used to build it, are addressed by separate standards in the same series.
D66: Cyber security requirements for I&C systems
Requirements for computer security of nuclear I&C, and how they relate to the safety classification.
It does not replace the site security plan.
D67: quality management for the supply of nuclear items and services
Addresses the quality management expectations placed on a nuclear supply chain, including the integrity of items passing through it.
Certification against it describes the supplier, not the item, and confers no safety class.
D68: ventilation and confinement for nuclear installations other than reactors
Addresses how confinement and ventilation are designed for fuel cycle, waste and laboratory installations.
It does not cover the containment envelope of a power reactor, and reactor ventilation runs through a separate standard.
D69: Structural design of buildings and civil works
The European structural design suite, used on nuclear sites for items outside the safety classes and as the loading basis alongside nuclear codes.
They contain no nuclear-specific loading or acceptance criteria.
D70: The generic quality management system standard, used as the base layer under nuclear-specific quality requirements.
On its own it is not accepted as a nuclear quality programme.
D71: European utility requirements for LWR nuclear power plants
A utility-side requirement set for standard designs, used as a bid specification basis and as the basis for assessing how far a specific design meets it.
It is not a regulation and it confers no licensability; it also does not decide which design code applies.
D72: A US utility-side requirement set for advanced light water reactors.
Access is restricted and it has no regulatory standing.
D73: Peer-derived operating performance expectations used by the operating fleet.
Membership material, not a public benchmark, and not a licensing instrument.
D74: Consolidated technical positions and international benchmarks in areas where standards are still forming.
Evidence and method. It requires nothing.
D75: Method-level material supporting the safety standards, including worked approaches and benchmark exercises.
Explicitly non-binding, and not maintained in step with the safety standards.
D76: The analysis route for transients and design basis accidents in water-cooled systems.
A code is not a requirement. Its validation matrix and its applicability to your plant are what the file has to establish.
D77: The analysis route for core degradation, containment behaviour and source term in design extension conditions.
Phenomenological uncertainty is large and is part of the result, not a defect of it.
D78: The analysis route for core physics, depletion, shielding source terms and criticality safety.
Validation against critical experiments representative of your configuration is what makes a result usable.
D79: The method for deriving site ground motion hazard, including the treatment of expert judgement and uncertainty.
The method does not fix the design ground motion. That is a regulatory and design decision.
D80: The analysis route from a release to off-site dose, used for permitting, for accident analysis and for emergency planning.
Model choice and the meteorological data set dominate the answer, so the justification of both belongs in the file with the result.
IA01: fundamental safety objective and the principles beneath every other standard

States the single safety objective and the set of principles from which all IAEA Safety Requirements are derived, including the primacy of the operator's responsibility and the role of defence in depth.
It contains no criterion that a design can be tested against; the principles only become checkable through the Requirements publications and through whatever a national regime has adopted.
IA02: governmental, legal and regulatory framework for safety

What a state has to establish before a nuclear facility can be authorised: an effectively independent regulatory body, a licensing and inspection system, and a clear allocation of prime responsibility to the licensee.
It is addressed to the state and the regulator, not to a designer or operator, so a project cannot demonstrate conformity with it; and it has no effect until national legislation gives it one.
IA03: What an organisation responsible for a facility has to put in place as an integrated management system, and what leadership for safety and safety culture are expected to look like in practice.

It is not a certifiable standard and it is not quality assurance in the older sense; an ISO 9001 or ISO 19443 certificate says nothing about conformity with it, and it prescribes no document hierarchy.
IA04: international basic safety standards for radiation protection
The framework of planned, existing and emergency exposure situations, dose limits and constraints, justification and optimisation, and the responsibilities that come with each.

It sets protection outcomes, not engineering: no shielding thicknesses, ventilation regimes or effluent design targets follow from it, and inside the EU the transposed Basic Safety Standards Directive rather than this text is the binding instrument.
IA05: safety assessment for facilities and activities
What a safety assessment has to cover, how it is graded, and the requirement that it be independently verified and kept current through the facility's life.
It requires that assessment be done but prescribes no acceptance criteria, no analysis methods, no initiating event list and no validation basis for the computer codes used.
IA06: How waste is to be managed from generation through characterisation, treatment, conditioning and storage up to the point at which it is accepted for disposal, including waste minimisation at the design stage.
It stops at the boundary of disposal: the waste acceptance criteria that actually constrain conditioning come from the receiving storage or disposal facility's own safety case, not from here.
IA07: The requirement to plan for decommissioning from the design stage, to maintain and update that plan, and to complete decommissioning within a defined strategy rather than deferring indefinitely.

It sets no end-state or site release criteria; what counts as an acceptable final condition is decided nationally, informed by clearance guidance, and it does not cover legacy sites never formally licensed.
IA08: preparedness and response for a nuclear or radiological emergency
The arrangements a state, a regulator and an operator need across all emergency preparedness categories, from hazard assessment through protective actions to transition back to normal.
It does not fix emergency planning zone sizes, protective action levels or operational intervention levels; those come from applying the criteria guidance within a national arrangement.
IA09: generic criteria and operational intervention levels for emergency decisions
How dose criteria are turned into things a decision maker can actually observe, so that protective actions can be triggered on measurable quantities rather than on reconstructed dose.
The numbers are generic starting points for a national framework, not thresholds a facility can adopt directly, and the guide does not size planning zones or design monitoring networks.
IA10: How an employer arranges dose assessment, workplace monitoring, classification of areas, health surveillance and optimisation for workers exposed at a nuclear facility.

It concerns the programme rather than the engineering: the shielding, ventilation and layout decisions that determine the doses are settled in the design guides, and dose constraints are a national matter.
IA11: radiation protection of the public and the environment
How the representative person is defined, how public exposure pathways are assessed, and how protection of the environment as such is handled alongside protection of people.
It does not authorise any discharge and does not supply the environmental transfer models or habit data; discharge authorisation is a national permitting act taken on site-specific evidence.
IA12: regulatory control of radioactive discharges to the environment
How a regulator should set, authorise and then control discharges of radioactive substances to air and water, including the role of source-related constraints and reporting.
It provides no discharge limits and no dispersion or dose modelling; it also does not deal with non-radiological discharges, which are permitted under separate environmental law.
IA13: How the radiological part of an environmental impact assessment is carried out before a facility is authorised, covering normal operation and accident conditions and impacts on people and biota.

It covers only the radiological chapter: conventional impacts, cumulative effects, alternatives assessment and the public participation procedure come from national environmental law and, in Europe, the EIA Directive.
IA14: remediation of areas affected by past activities or events
How a remediation strategy is developed for an existing exposure situation, from characterisation of the contaminated area to the justification and optimisation of the remedial option chosen.
It addresses existing exposure situations, not the planned decommissioning of a licensed facility, and it sets no cleanup concentration or dose target; those are set case by case by the regulator.
IA15: application of the concept of clearance
How materials and items arising from a licensed practice can be released from regulatory control, and what has to be demonstrated about the activity concentration and the release route.

Clearance levels have effect only once a national regulator adopts them, and the guide does not settle measurement methods, sampling strategies or how a consignment is verified before it leaves the site.
IA16: leadership, management and culture for safety

How the leadership and management system requirements are implemented in practice, including safety culture characteristics, organisational change control and the integration of safety with other objectives.

It offers no auditable safety culture criteria and no scoring scheme; a self-assessment against it is evidence of reflection, not of performance, and it does not replace contractual quality requirements.
IA17: management system arrangements specific to nuclear installations
How the generic management system expectations are applied to the phases of a nuclear installation, from siting and design through construction, commissioning, operation and decommissioning.
It was written against the management system requirements that have since been replaced, so it has to be read alongside the current leadership and management requirements rather than used on its own.
IA18: What has to be evaluated about a site: external natural and human-induced hazards, the site's capacity to allow radioactive material dispersion and emergency response, and the effects of the installation on the region.

It governs evaluation of a chosen site rather than selection between candidates, and it supplies no screening distances, return periods or exclusion criteria - those come from the hazard guides and national rules.
IA19: design requirements for nuclear power plant safety

The full set of design requirements for a power reactor: safety functions, defence in depth levels, design basis accidents, design extension conditions, and the treatment of common cause failure and human factors.

It is written primarily for land-based stationary plants with water-cooled reactors, so its wording on core cooling, containment and postulated initiating events does not transfer unexamined to gas-cooled, fast or salt-fuelled designs.
IA20: commissioning and operation requirements for nuclear power plants

What is required of the operating organisation from the start of commissioning onwards: management of the plant, operational limits and conditions, maintenance, and the feedback of operating experience.
It does not give test acceptance criteria for commissioning, and it does not tell an operator how to structure technical specifications for a particular regulator's approval.
IA21: The requirements covering design, commissioning, operation, utilisation and decommissioning of reactors run for research, training and isotope production, including their experimental devices.

It is not a scaled-down power reactor standard and not the reverse: applying it to a power reactor understates what is expected, and accelerator-driven isotope facilities without a critical core fall outside it entirely.
IA22: safety requirements for nuclear fuel cycle facilities

The requirements for facilities that convert, enrich, fabricate, reprocess or otherwise handle nuclear material outside a reactor, with confinement and criticality control as the dominant safety functions.

It excludes uranium mining and milling and excludes disposal facilities, and it is not a reactor standard: importing reactor concepts such as design basis accident lists into a chemical plant misreads it.
IA23: safety requirements for disposal of radioactive waste
What is required of any disposal facility - near surface, borehole or geological - in terms of passive safety, multiple barriers, the safety case and the period after closure.

It deliberately does not choose between disposal concepts or host rocks, and it fixes neither the assessment time frame, the dose or risk constraint, nor the policy on retrievability and institutional control.
IA24: regulations for the safe transport of radioactive material
The package types, activity limits, test performance requirements and consignment controls that govern moving radioactive material by any mode.

It becomes binding only through the modal instruments and national transport law that adopt it, and it governs package safety rather than the physical protection of a shipment, which is a separate security regime.
IA25: How to build the seismotectonic model, characterise seismic sources and produce the ground motion hazard for a site, by both probabilistic and deterministic routes.

It produces hazard, not design input: the choice of hazard level, the return period and the way ground motion becomes a design basis earthquake are settled by the national regulator and the seismic design guide.
IA26: meteorological and hydrological hazards in site evaluation
How extreme wind, precipitation, temperature, snow, storm surge, tsunami, river flood and dam-related flooding are characterised for a site.
It does not settle how these hazards are combined with each other or with seismic loading, nor how margin beyond the design basis is demonstrated - the areas most often challenged in review.
IA27: site survey and site selection for nuclear installations
How a region is screened and candidate sites are compared and ranked before any one of them is taken forward for full evaluation.

Ranking sites under this guide does not discharge the site evaluation requirements, and it says nothing about land acquisition, grid connection, cooling water rights or public acceptance, which usually decide the outcome.
IA28: hazards from human induced external events in site evaluation
How accidental external hazards created by people - aircraft crash, industrial explosion, toxic release, transport accidents near the site - are identified and characterised.

It deals with accidental events only; deliberate acts including malicious aircraft impact are handled through the design basis threat and the security series, and a screening-out argument here carries no weight there.
IA29: site characteristics and radiation risks to the public and environment in site evaluation
How atmospheric and aquatic dispersion, population distribution and land and water use around a site are investigated and used to assess radiation risk during site evaluation.

It informs the assessment but authorises nothing: it does not set discharge limits and does not determine emergency planning zones, and its dispersion treatment is for site evaluation rather than for accident consequence analysis.
IA30: geotechnical aspects of siting and design
How site soil and rock conditions are investigated, how liquefaction, slope stability and settlement are assessed, and how soil-structure interaction inputs are prepared for design.

It stops at the geotechnical input: foundation and structural design itself is governed by whatever civil code the project adopts, and it does not settle acceptance criteria for differential settlement or bearing capacity.
IA31: deterministic safety analysis for nuclear power plants
How deterministic analyses are classified and used, the difference between conservative, best-estimate and best-estimate-plus-uncertainty approaches, and what each is appropriate for.

It gives no acceptance criteria, no initiating event frequencies and no validation requirement for a particular thermal-hydraulic code; a code qualified for one plant and phenomenon is not thereby qualified for another.
IA32: How to build, quality-assure and apply a Level 1 model covering internal events, internal hazards and external hazards, including at-power and shutdown states.
It sets no core damage frequency target - that is a national or utility decision - and it neither qualifies PSA software nor settles how a model is used in risk-informed decisions.
IA33: How the Level 1 result is carried through containment performance and severe accident phenomena to source terms, release categories and their frequencies.
It stops at release: off-site consequence and risk to the public is Level 3 work, large release and large early release definitions vary between regimes, and the frequency targets are set nationally.
IA34: format and content of the safety analysis report
What chapters a safety analysis report is expected to contain and what belongs in each, so that a regulator can find the argument and the supporting evidence.

It gives structure rather than substance, and a regulator with its own submission format - a US style final safety analysis report, a UK safety case, a French rapport de sûreté - will expect that instead.
IA35: safety classification of structures, systems and components
A method for deriving safety classes from the safety functions an item performs, the consequence of its failure and the plant states in which it is needed.

It does not map the resulting classes onto engineering codes, so the link to ASME III classes, RCC-M levels, IEC categories or seismic categories is still a project decision that the regulator will probe.
IA36: design extension conditions and practical elimination
How design extension conditions are selected and analysed, and what an argument for practical elimination of a large or early release has to contain to be credible.

It declares no sequence practically eliminated and offers no frequency cut-off below which a sequence can be dismissed; the claim always has to be made for the specific design, with physical rather than probabilistic argument.
IA37: How core design demonstrates control of reactivity, adequate thermal margins, fuel integrity limits and core monitoring capability across operational states and accident conditions.

It is built around water-cooled cores; its treatment of reactivity coefficients, departure from nucleate boiling and core instrumentation does not carry over to fast, gas-cooled or molten-salt cores without rederivation.
IA38: design of the reactor containment and associated systems
How the containment function is designed: leaktightness and leak rate testing, isolation, pressure suppression, heat removal, hydrogen management and penetrations.

It addresses the functional design, not the structural analysis and construction of the concrete or steel shell, which follow a civil or mechanical code; and it does not settle containment performance criteria under severe accident loads.
IA39: design of the reactor coolant system and associated systems
How the reactor coolant pressure boundary and its auxiliaries are designed for integrity, overpressure protection, inspectability and the prevention of loss of coolant.

It is not a pressure vessel code: stress analysis rules, material specifications, welding and manufacturing requirements come from ASME III, RCC-M, KTA or an equivalent that a licence or contract adopts.
IA40: design of auxiliary and supporting systems
How ventilation and air conditioning, cooling water, compressed air, fire water and similar service systems are designed when they support safety functions.

It works at a functional level: filtration efficiencies, duct and housing classification, filter qualification and in-place testing come from separate standards, and confinement design for non-reactor facilities is outside its scope.
IA41: protection against internal hazards in design
How internal fire, explosion, flooding, pipe whip, jet impingement, dropped loads and internal missiles are identified and how the design protects safety functions against them.

It supplies no fire load calculation method, no barrier rating scheme and no fire modelling validation basis; a fire hazard analysis still rests on national fire codes and on separate deterministic or probabilistic fire methods.
IA42: How off-site and on-site power, emergency supplies, distribution architecture, independence and the loss of off-site power case are handled in the design of a power reactor.

It stops at architecture and function: equipment ratings, protection coordination, cable sizing and qualification testing follow IEC or IEEE standards that the project adopts, and grid code obligations are separate.
IA43: design of instrumentation and control systems
How the overall I&C architecture is arranged - protection system, control system, defence in depth between layers, independence, diversity and the treatment of common cause software failure.
It does not replace the IEC 61513 and IEC 60880 family, where software development rigour, tool qualification, pre-developed software justification and independent assessment are actually specified.
IA44: human factors engineering in the design of nuclear power plants
How a human factors engineering programme runs through design, from function allocation and task analysis to control room design and integrated system validation.

It sets no control room ergonomic, alarm-handling or workload criteria; those come from standards and from the detailed human-system interface guidance that regulators such as the NRC publish separately.
IA45: How seismic categorisation is assigned and how structures, systems and components are designed and analysed for the design basis earthquake, including seismic interaction and margin considerations.

It gives approach rather than rules: acceptance criteria, load combinations, damping values and detailing come from the civil and mechanical codes the project adopts, and it does not cover seismic PSA methods.
IA46: design against external events other than earthquakes
How the design accommodates extreme wind, flood, extreme temperature, aircraft crash, external explosion and combinations of these, including the protection strategy and site layout measures.

It relies entirely on hazard parameters produced under the site evaluation guides, and it does not define load combinations or the margin to be shown beyond the design basis, which regulators increasingly ask for explicitly.
IA47: How equipment is qualified for the environmental, seismic, electromagnetic and ageing conditions it will face, and how the qualified condition is preserved through procurement, installation and life.

It describes the programme, not the test method: sequences, ageing acceleration models, margins and documentation formats come from IEC and IEEE qualification standards, and it does not address commercial grade dedication.
IA48: How layout, shielding, source term reduction, material choice, decontamination provisions and access control are used at the design stage to keep occupational exposure low.
It offers no shielding calculation method, no source terms and no dose constraint; and being the newest of the design guides, it has yet to be reflected in most existing design bases.
IA49: criticality safety in the handling of fissile material
How subcriticality is assured outside reactors: the double contingency principle, choice of controlled parameters, criticality safety assessment and the alarm and response arrangements.

It contains no subcritical limits and no validated data; the burden of validating the criticality code against benchmarks relevant to the actual materials, geometry and moderation stays with the analyst.
IA50: safety management of construction for nuclear installations
How safety is managed during construction and installation: control of the design authority interface, nonconformance handling, configuration control and the transfer of systems to commissioning.
It does not cover conventional construction health and safety law, and it is not a supply chain quality standard - NQA-1, ISO 19443 or the contract's own regime govern that.
IA51: How the commissioning programme is structured into stages, how test results are reviewed against design intent, and how responsibility passes from constructor to operating organisation.

It supplies no test acceptance criteria; those come from the design authority and the safety analysis, and the guide does not settle how much of first-of-a-kind testing a regulator will require before fuel load.
IA52: operational limits and conditions and operating procedures
How limits and conditions are derived from the safety analysis, how they are expressed as surveillance requirements and actions, and how operating procedures relate to them.
It contains no limit values and does not settle the format a given regulator will accept for technical specifications, nor the treatment of allowed outage times and completion times.
IA53: protection against internal and external hazards in operation

How hazard protection is maintained once the plant is running: fire protection programme, combustible control, hot work, flood and severe weather preparation, and the management of temporary conditions.

It is the operational companion to the design hazard guides and does not settle fire brigade staffing, insurer requirements or compliance with the national fire code that applies to the site as a workplace.
IA54: How an accident management programme is developed and maintained, covering preventive and mitigatory guidance, the transition between procedures and guidelines, and the technical support arrangements.

The plant-specific severe accident management guidelines, their computational basis and their validation are not in it, and it does not settle the boundary between the control room and the emergency organisation.
IA55: How a comprehensive review against a set of safety factors is scoped, conducted and turned into an improvement programme, typically to support continued or long term operation.

It sets neither the review interval nor the standard against which the plant is compared; some regimes use continuous review instead, and the outcome of a review binds nothing until the regulator accepts it.
IA56: ageing management and preparation for long term operation
How degradation mechanisms are screened, how ageing management programmes are built for structures and components, and what a long term operation assessment has to demonstrate.

It gives programme structure only: the degradation mechanisms, inspection intervals, acceptance criteria and time-limited ageing analyses for a given component come from the in-service inspection code and plant-specific evaluation.
IA57: radiation safety of accelerator based radioisotope production facilities

How a cyclotron or linac isotope production facility is designed and run for shielding, activation of structures and of the air, target and hot cell handling, ventilation and the resulting waste streams.

It does not cover the medical or industrial use of the product once it leaves the facility, and the activation inventories and shielding still need facility-specific modelling that no guide can supply.
IA58: safety infrastructure for a new nuclear power programme
What safety-related capability a newcomer state has to build and in what order, from legal framework and regulator through to operator competence and emergency arrangements.
It is written for the state, not for a vendor or investor; it is not a project schedule, and it deliberately leaves aside grid, financing, industrial capability and workforce economics.
IA59: safety assessment and safety analysis report for research reactors
How the safety assessment for a research reactor is scoped and graded, and how the resulting safety analysis report is structured.

Its expectations are scaled to research reactor hazard potential; meeting it does not meet the deterministic and probabilistic expectations that power reactor guidance sets, and the reverse import is equally wrong.
IA60: graded application of the safety requirements to research reactors
How the research reactor safety requirements are applied proportionately to power, source term, experimental complexity and site, so that a low-power facility is not treated like a high-flux one.

Grading is a way of proportioning effort, not of setting requirements aside; the graded outcome still has to be justified and accepted by the regulator, and there is no threshold below which requirements disappear.
IA61: instrumentation, control and software for research reactors
How protection and control systems and their software are designed, verified and maintained at a research reactor, including the use of commercially available equipment.

Its expectations are lighter than the power reactor route through the design I&C guide and IEC 61513, so conformity here supports no claim for a power reactor system or for a fuel cycle facility protection system.
IA62: radiation protection and waste management in research reactor design and operation
How shielding, ventilation, containment of experiments, contamination control and waste arisings are handled for a reactor with frequent experimental and irradiation work.
It covers the reactor and its experimental devices; hot cells, radioisotope processing laboratories and accelerator facilities sharing the site fall under other standards with different expectations.
IA63: How commissioning stages, test programmes, initial criticality and power ascension are planned and controlled for a research reactor, including recommissioning after major modification.
It does not supply test acceptance criteria, and it does not address commissioning of experimental devices installed later in life, which is handled under utilisation and modification arrangements.
IA64: safety of conversion and uranium enrichment facilities
How conversion and enrichment plants are designed and operated for confinement, criticality control, and the chemical hazards that dominate the risk in these facilities.
The chemical process safety regime - major accident hazard law such as Seveso as transposed, and the associated hazard studies - runs in parallel and is not discharged by following this guide.
IA65: safety of uranium fuel fabrication facilities
How a uranium fuel fabrication plant controls criticality, confinement, fire and chemical hazards through powder handling, pellet production, rod loading and assembly.
It is written for uranium; plutonium-bearing fabrication is covered separately, and neither guide supplies criticality limits, glovebox design values or filtration performance.
IA66: safety of mixed oxide fuel fabrication facilities
How the additional hazards of plutonium-bearing fabrication are handled: glovebox containment, alpha contamination control, criticality with mixed fissile species and decay heat in stored material.

It does not address safeguards obligations or physical protection of separated plutonium, which arise from the safeguards agreement and the security series and often drive the plant layout more than safety does.
IA67: safety of nuclear fuel reprocessing facilities
How a reprocessing plant handles the combination of criticality, solvent fire and red oil, hydrogen, high decay heat and multi-barrier confinement across a long chemical flowsheet.

It covers the separation plant; downstream vitrification, product and waste storage, and transport of separated material are governed by other standards, and it gives no confinement or filtration performance values.
IA68: How wet and dry spent fuel storage is designed and operated for heat removal, subcriticality, retrievability, cladding integrity and monitoring over long storage periods.

It is generic across storage types: cask design, cladding temperature and hydride reorientation criteria, burnup credit and the licensing of a specific cask system are settled through national cask approval routes.
IA69: How waste from a power reactor or research reactor is characterised, segregated, treated, conditioned and stored, and how waste generation is minimised by design and operating practice.

It does not contain the waste acceptance criteria that actually constrain conditioning choices; those belong to the receiving storage or disposal facility and often do not yet exist when the plant is designed.
IA70: decommissioning of reactors and fuel cycle facilities
How decommissioning is planned and executed: characterisation, strategy selection between immediate and deferred dismantling, dose and waste optimisation, and the final survey.
It does not fix the end state or the release criteria for the site, and it does not cover remediation of legacy contamination that was never part of a licensed facility.
IA71: How a deep geological disposal facility is sited, designed, constructed, operated and closed, and how the engineered and natural barriers are argued to work together after closure.

It is host-rock neutral and does not choose between clay, granite and salt concepts; it also leaves retrievability policy, the duration of institutional control and the disposal inventory to national decision.
IA72: How a near surface facility is sited, designed and operated, how the cover system and institutional control period are treated, and how inadvertent human intrusion is addressed.
It supplies no waste acceptance criteria or activity limits; those follow from the facility's own post-closure safety assessment, and it does not settle how long-lived waste is excluded in practice.
IA73: the safety case and safety assessment for disposal
How a disposal safety case is structured, how scenarios are developed, and how uncertainty, the biosphere and very long timescales are handled in the assessment.

It fixes neither the assessment time frame nor the dose or risk criterion, both of which are national; and a safety case built to it still stands or falls on site-specific data that no guide can supply.
IA74: advisory material for the transport regulations
Paragraph-by-paragraph explanation of the intent behind the transport regulations, including how test conditions, activity limits and package approval provisions are meant to be read.
It has no regulatory force of its own, and it is keyed to the previous revision of the regulations rather than the current one, so parts of it no longer track the text it explains.
IA75: format and content of the package design safety report
What a package design safety report has to contain so that a competent authority can review structural, thermal, containment, shielding and criticality performance.
It defines structure, not demonstration: the test performance and analysis that prove the package come from the transport regulations and from the competent authority's own approval practice.
IA76: emergency preparedness and response for transport accidents
How emergency arrangements are made for accidents in transport, where the responder, the carrier, the consignor and the state each hold part of the response.
It does not replace site emergency arrangements, and it does not discharge the carrier's obligations under modal transport law, which impose their own reporting and response duties.
IA77: recommendations on physical protection of nuclear material and facilities
The recommended physical protection regime for nuclear material in use, storage and transport and for facilities, built around categorisation of material and graded protection levels.

It is a recommendation rather than a treaty text - binding obligations come from the amended physical protection convention and national law - and it defines no threat, since that is the state's design basis threat.
IA78: national threat assessment and design basis threat
How a state carries out a nuclear security threat assessment and turns it into a design basis threat or representative threat statement that operators can design against.
The threat itself is a national and usually classified document; nothing in this guide lets a project derive adversary capability, and protection designed from the guide alone will not be accepted.
IA79: implementing physical protection at nuclear facilities
How the physical protection recommendations are put into practice: detection, delay and response functions, security zones, insider mitigation and the security management system.

It leaves material categorisation decisions, vital area identification, response force performance requirements and performance testing standards to the national regulator, and its measures are not a substitute for the design basis threat.
IA80: security through the lifetime of a nuclear facility
How security is built in from concept through design, construction, commissioning, operation and decommissioning, rather than added to a completed design.

It does not resolve the conflicts between security, safety and safeguards that a project has to arbitrate, and it gives no criteria for judging when a security-driven design change degrades a safety function.
IA81: How a computer security programme is established at state and facility level, including risk management, the graded approach and the relationship between computer security and physical protection.
It is a programme guide, not a control catalogue, and it does not replace IEC 62645 or an equivalent national cyber security standard for instrumentation and control.
IA82: computer security of instrumentation and control systems
Technical measures for protecting I&C systems at nuclear facilities: zoning, data flow control, secure development, supply chain and maintenance of computer security through life.
It does not settle how security zones map onto safety classes, nor how a security-driven modification to a protection system is justified against the existing safety case.
IA83: security of nuclear material in transport
How shipments of nuclear material are protected: consignor and carrier responsibilities, transport security plans, communication, and the graded response to categorisation.
It says nothing about package safety design, which belongs to the transport regulations, and route approval, escort arrangements and armed response remain state decisions.
IA84: nuclear material accounting and control used for security purposes
How the material accountancy and control system at a facility can be used to detect and deter unauthorised removal, complementing physical protection.
Using accountancy for security does not discharge safeguards obligations, which are verified by the IAEA under a separate legal instrument with its own measurement and reporting requirements.
IA85: How a reactor design can be made easier to safeguard - material flow visibility, containment and surveillance provision, access for inspectors, design information declaration.

It is guidance, not a requirement, and it does not state what the IAEA will actually require at a given facility; that is settled through the safeguards agreement, design information questionnaire and facility attachment.
UK01: the statute that created the nuclear regulator and its powers

Who regulates nuclear safety, security, safeguards and nuclear-site health and safety in Great Britain, what enforcement instruments that regulator holds, and how nuclear regulatory requirements are made and amended.

It creates the regulator and the enforcement machinery but sets almost no technical requirement itself; what a plant has to achieve comes from the licence conditions, the relevant regulations and the safety case made under them.
UK02: nuclear site licensing and operator liability for nuclear damage

Which installations may not be operated without a nuclear site licence, who may hold one, what the licensing regime attaches to the site, and the operator's strict liability and cover obligations for nuclear damage.

It says the regulator may attach such conditions as it thinks fit but does not itself state a single design or operating requirement, and holding a licence settles nothing about permits for discharges, planning consent or security approvals.
UK03: general duties on employers and designers, and the reasonable practicability test

What general duties fall on employers, the self-employed, controllers of premises and designers of articles for use at work, and what the qualifier 'so far as is reasonably practicable' obliges a duty holder to weigh.

The reasonable-practicability test is the yardstick but the Act gives no method for demonstrating it; the balance of risk against sacrifice has to be argued case by case, and the Act does not displace the more specific radiation and nuclear regulations.
UK04: dose limitation, restriction of exposure and radiation employer duties

What an employer working with ionising radiation has to do about justification, optimisation, dose limits, designation of controlled and supervised areas, contingency plans, monitoring, and appointment of radiation protection advisers.

It governs occupational and public exposure from a practice but does not settle plant design questions such as shielding layout, source term or the classification of protection systems; those come from the safety case and from nuclear-specific guidance.
UK05: operator and local authority duties for radiation emergencies

What hazard evaluation, consequence assessment, emergency planning zones, on-site and off-site plans, prior information to the public and testing arrangements are required where a radiation emergency is reasonably foreseeable.

It drives the size of planning areas from a consequences assessment but does not prescribe the accident sequences to be analysed, nor does it approve the design measures that make an emergency less likely.
UK06: environmental permitting for radioactive substances activities in England and Wales

What activities involving radioactive substances, disposal of radioactive waste and other regulated facilities require an environmental permit, who grants and enforces it, and what standard permit machinery such as variation, transfer and surrender applies.

The permit regime controls discharge and disposal routes; it does not authorise nuclear operation, does not deal with worker dose, and its surrender provisions are not the same thing as ending the nuclear site licence.
UK07: the Scottish route for authorising radioactive substances activities

How radioactive substances activities and radioactive waste disposals are authorised in Scotland under the integrated environmental authorisation framework, and which tier of authorisation a given activity falls into.

It is the Scottish counterpart of the English and Welsh permitting regime rather than an add-on, so a project has to establish which jurisdiction governs its site before assuming the English permit structure and its guidance transfer.
UK08: security of nuclear premises, nuclear material and sensitive nuclear information

What approved security plan a responsible person for nuclear premises has to have, how transport of nuclear material within Great Britain is controlled, and what duties attach to sensitive nuclear information and to carriers.

It requires an approved plan without setting out in public what the plan has to contain; the substantive expectations sit in the regulator's security assessment principles and in threat information that is not openly published.
UK09: domestic nuclear material accountancy, control and reporting
What records, accounting and operating records, reports and notifications an operator of a qualifying nuclear facility owes the regulator so that the state can account for civil nuclear material.
Safeguards accountancy answers questions about material inventory and flow; it settles nothing about criticality safety, physical protection or export control, which run on separate legal tracks.
UK10: the power to create and run a domestic safeguards regime
How the state took power to establish civil nuclear safeguards obligations in domestic law and to give effect to international agreements on safeguards after leaving the Euratom arrangements.

It is enabling legislation; the operational duties on a facility are in the safeguards regulations made under it, and it does not itself describe measurement, containment or surveillance expectations.
UK11: the consenting route for nationally significant energy infrastructure

How a development consent order is applied for and examined for infrastructure that meets the nationally significant threshold, what pre-application consultation is required, and how designated national policy statements bear on the decision.

Development consent deals with land use, environmental effects and compulsory acquisition; it neither licenses nuclear operation nor permits radioactive discharges, and a granted order does not shorten the nuclear licensing route.
UK12: the ordinary planning route for development not caught by the infrastructure regime
When planning permission is needed for development, how applications are decided against the development plan, and what conditions and obligations may be attached.

Many nuclear-related works fall outside the nationally significant infrastructure thresholds and land here instead; the Act gives no radiological criteria, and a planning permission carries no weight in the nuclear safety case.
UK13: designated national planning policy for nuclear energy generation

What policy the decision maker on a development consent application for nuclear generating infrastructure is required to apply, including the approach to need, siting criteria and the assessment of impacts.

Designated policy shapes the planning decision only; it does not determine whether a design is acceptable to the nuclear or environmental regulators, and site suitability in planning terms is not the same as the site evaluation done for the safety case.
UK14: environmental impact assessment before a reactor is dismantled
What environmental statement and consent process a licensee has to complete before beginning to dismantle or decommission a nuclear reactor, and what the regulator considers before granting consent.

The consent covers the environmental effects of the decommissioning project; it does not approve the decommissioning safety case, does not authorise waste disposals, and does not release the site from regulatory control.
UK15: the prior justification decision for a new class or type of practice
Whether the economic, social and other benefits of a new class or type of practice involving ionising radiation outweigh its health detriment, and who takes that decision as justifying authority.

Justification is a decision about a class or type of practice, taken by a minister, not a technical approval of a particular design or site; a justified practice still faces the whole licensing, permitting and consenting sequence.
UK16: carriage of radioactive material by road, rail and inland waterway

How the international modal rules for the carriage of dangerous goods, including Class 7 radioactive material, take effect in domestic law, and what duties fall on consignors, carriers, drivers and vehicle operators.

It gives legal force to package and consignment rules but does not itself contain the package design and test criteria, and it is distinct from the security requirements that apply to the same movement.
UK17: funded decommissioning programmes and the geological disposal framework

What a person proposing to build a new nuclear power station has to put in place to secure funding for decommissioning and waste management, and what statutory framework supports a geological disposal facility.
Approval of a funding programme is a financial and institutional judgement; it says nothing about the technical adequacy of the decommissioning strategy or the waste routes assumed in it.
UK18: general fire safety duties for premises and the responsible person

What fire risk assessment, general fire precautions, means of escape, maintenance and information duties fall on the responsible person for non-domestic premises, and who enforces them on nuclear licensed sites.

It addresses general fire safety for the protection of people from fire; it does not address fire as a nuclear safety hazard, so it settles nothing about fire-induced initiating events, segregation of redundant trains or passive fire protection of safety systems.
UK19: the standard conditions attached to every nuclear site licence

What standing obligations run with a nuclear site licence across marking of the site, documents and records, training, examination and maintenance, operating rules, safety cases, modifications, emergency arrangements, decommissioning and organisational capability.

Almost every condition requires the licensee to make and implement adequate arrangements without stating what those arrangements have to contain, so compliance is judged against the licensee's own arrangements and its safety case, not against the text of the condition.
UK20: the regulator's principles for judging a nuclear safety case

What an inspector looks for when judging whether a safety case demonstrates that risks have been reduced so far as is reasonably practicable, across leadership, fault analysis, engineering principles, radiological protection and numerical targets.
They are principles for assessment, not design rules and not law; meeting them is neither claimed nor accepted as automatic acceptance, and departures are permitted where the safety case argues them.
UK21: the regulator's principles for judging nuclear security arrangements

What outcomes a dutyholder's security arrangements are expected to deliver across leadership, culture, competence, procurement, reliability, risk assessment, cyber and information security, personnel security, response and physical protection.

They describe expected security outcomes rather than prescribing protective measures, and they do not by themselves reconcile security measures with the safety case where the two pull in opposite directions.
UK22: how a reactor design is put through generic design assessment

What a requesting party has to submit, how the step structure of generic design assessment works, how the joint programme office and the regulators interact with the requesting party, and what the possible outcomes of the process are.

Generic design assessment is a voluntary process about a generic design; it is not a licence, it does not authorise construction, and its outcome does not remove the site-specific safety case, permits and consents needed later.
UK23: technical expectations for submissions made in generic design assessment

How the regulator expects the technical content of a generic safety and security case to be structured, scoped and substantiated at each step, and how claims, arguments and evidence are expected to develop.

It sets expectations for the generic submission; it does not fix the acceptability of any technical position, and generic exclusions and assumptions carried through the process become site-specific work that the guidance does not resolve.
UK24: what makes a safety case adequate and how it is maintained

What a safety case is for, what claims, arguments and evidence structure the regulator expects, how it is kept alive through the plant lifecycle, and how the regulator judges its adequacy at permissioning points.
It is guidance to inspectors on judging safety cases, not a specification of contents; it does not tell an operator which analyses to perform or which acceptance criteria to adopt.
UK25: reducing risk so far as is reasonably practicable in regulatory decisions
How the duty to reduce risks is regulated in practice, how gross disproportion between sacrifice and risk reduction is argued, and how relevant good practice and numerical targets feed the judgement.

It gives the reasoning framework, not the answer: it does not state what level of risk is acceptable for a given plant, and citing it does not by itself demonstrate that options have been properly considered.
UK26: design basis analysis of fault sequences

What set of initiating faults should be identified, how conservative assumptions and single failure should be applied, and what the analysis has to show about the protection provided by safety measures.
It is about the deterministic design basis and does not cover sequences beyond it; it also does not endorse any particular computer code, correlation set or plant data as validated for the duty.
UK27: analysis of accidents beyond the design basis

How severe accident behaviour, the phenomena involved, mitigation measures and accident management are expected to be addressed in a safety case, and what the regulator looks for in the supporting analysis.

It addresses the demonstration, not the design: it does not prescribe severe accident features, containment survivability criteria or the boundary between design extension conditions and severe accidents for a given plant.
UK28: assessment of hazards originating outside the facility
How natural and human-induced external hazards are identified, screened, characterised and combined, and how the resulting loads and effects should be carried into design and the safety case.
It does not provide site data, hazard curves or return-period values for any location; site characterisation and the derivation of design basis events remain the operator's work.
UK29: assessment of hazards originating inside the facility

How internal fire, flood, explosion, missiles, dropped loads, pipe failure and similar internal hazards are identified, screened and analysed, and how layout, segregation and protection are judged against them.

This is the main route by which nuclear fire safety is assessed, but it is inspector guidance rather than a fire code: it sets no fire resistance periods, separation distances or suppression requirements.
UK30: structural integrity of metal components and the highest reliability claims

How claims on the integrity of metal structures, systems and components are substantiated, including design, manufacture, defect tolerance, inspection and the treatment of components whose failure cannot be tolerated.
It concerns the substantiation of integrity claims and does not adopt any single design or construction code; whether a chosen code plus supplements supports the claim still has to be argued.
UK31: assessment of civil engineering structures on nuclear sites
How the design, analysis, construction, examination and maintenance of nuclear safety-related civil structures are judged, including materials, ground conditions, loading combinations and durability.
It is not a design code and gives no load factors or detailing rules; the adequacy of the chosen structural code and of site-specific ground and hazard input remains to be demonstrated.
UK32: How supporting services such as power, cooling, compressed air and service water that safety systems depend on are identified, classified, provided with redundancy and diversity, and substantiated.
It deals with the adequacy of support services rather than the process systems they serve, and it does not settle how far common support systems undermine claimed independence between trains.
UK33: confinement and containment of radioactive material
How containment and confinement functions across nuclear facilities are claimed, engineered, tested and maintained, including barriers, penetrations, leakage and the interaction with ventilation.
It covers the confinement function generically and does not give leakage acceptance criteria, test pressures or containment design rules for any specific reactor type or facility.
UK34: ventilation systems as a safety measure
How ventilation and extract systems that provide confinement, depression, filtration and habitability are classified, designed, tested and maintained, and how their reliability is claimed.
It does not specify filter efficiencies, air change rates or pressure cascades; those come from the facility source term and the safety case, not from the guide.
UK35: management of radioactive waste on licensed sites
How waste is characterised, minimised, stored, conditioned and routed on a licensed site, and how the safety case for waste operations and passively safe storage is judged.

It addresses waste management from the nuclear safety standpoint on the licensed site; disposal routes, discharge limits and end-state acceptability are matters for the environment agencies and the disposal facility operator.
UK36: decommissioning strategy, planning and its safety case
How decommissioning strategy and programmes are judged, how hazard and risk reduction is prioritised, and what the regulator expects of the safety case for dismantling and hazard removal operations.
It concerns nuclear safety during decommissioning; it does not determine the site end state, does not settle land quality criteria and does not deliver release from regulatory control.
UK37: control and instrumentation aspects of bringing plant into service

How commissioning of control and instrumentation is planned and staged, how test evidence is used to confirm the claims made in the safety case, and how hold points and configuration control are handled.
It covers the control and instrumentation aspects rather than the whole commissioning programme, and it does not define the acceptance criteria that individual tests have to meet.
UK38: adequacy of probabilistic safety analysis models and their supporting analysis
How the scope, level, modelling assumptions, data, dependency treatment and quality of a probabilistic safety analysis are judged for the use being made of it.

It judges the model, not the plant: it does not state numerical risk criteria for acceptance, and an adequate model can still support a weak safety argument if the results are used beyond their scope.
UK39: How instrumentation and control systems that are relied on for safety, other than the highest-integrity protection systems, are categorised, designed, qualified and substantiated.
It does not resolve the split between systems assessed here and higher-integrity computer based protection, and it endorses no particular instrumentation standard as satisfying the claims.
UK40: radiological protection arrangements and their assessment
How dose reduction, optimisation, control of exposure, designation of areas, monitoring and radiological protection organisation on a nuclear facility are judged.
It is guidance on assessing arrangements, not a shielding or dosimetry method; it gives no design dose targets for particular areas and does not replace the statutory dose framework.
UK41: criticality safety of fissile material operations

How criticality safety assessments are scoped, what control mechanisms and the double contingency approach are expected to deliver, and how criticality safety limits and conditions are derived and controlled.
It does not validate any criticality code or cross-section library, and it does not give subcritical margins or safe values for particular geometries and enrichments.
UK42: computer based systems performing safety functions

How software-based protection and control systems are judged, including production excellence, independent confidence building, diversity from other systems and the treatment of pre-existing software.

It sets the assessment approach rather than adopting any software standard as sufficient evidence, and it does not resolve how much independent confidence building a particular reliability claim demands.
UK43: integrating human factors into design and modification
How human factors work is planned, scoped and integrated across a project so that the demands placed on people are analysed and reflected in design, procedures, staffing and training.

It describes the integration process rather than the human factors methods; it does not tell a project which analyses are proportionate to its risk or when the human factors evidence base is complete.
UK44: human reliability analysis in the safety case
How human failure events are identified, represented in deterministic and probabilistic analysis, quantified and supported by performance shaping factor and dependency treatment.

It endorses no single quantification technique and provides no human error probabilities; the credibility of a claimed recovery action still rests on plant-specific evidence such as timing, indications and training.
UK45: pressure systems safety on nuclear plant

How pressure systems and their protective devices are designed, examined, maintained and operated safely, and how conventional pressure system duties interact with nuclear safety claims on the same equipment.

It does not settle which pressure design code applies, and compliance with conventional pressure system duties does not discharge the structural integrity claims made on nuclear safety-related pressure boundaries.
UK46: supply chain arrangements for procuring safety related items and services

How a licensee's arrangements for specifying, selecting, controlling and assuring suppliers of nuclear safety related items and services are judged, including intelligent customer capability and oversight of lower tiers.
It concerns the licensee's arrangements rather than any supplier's management system, and third party certification of a supplier does not by itself answer the intelligent customer question.
UK47: categorising safety functions and classifying structures, systems and components

How safety functions are categorised by their significance and how the structures, systems and components delivering them are classified, and what that classification is expected to drive in codes, qualification and reliability.

Classification determines the engineering rigour expected but does not itself specify the codes, qualification programme or reliability targets that follow, and it does not settle the treatment of items with mixed safety and non-safety duties.
UK48: How the engineering of packages for radioactive material is assessed, including design substantiation, testing, manufacture, maintenance and the evidence supporting a package design approval.
It is the regulator's assessment guidance and not the package standard itself; it does not restate the test conditions or performance criteria that a package design has to meet.
UK49: emergency power generation and its reliability

How standby and emergency generating plant relied on in fault and accident conditions is specified, qualified, tested and maintained, and how its availability and reliability claims are substantiated.
It addresses the generating plant and its claims, not the wider electrical distribution architecture, and it does not state how long autonomy has to be provided for any plant.
UK50: managing ageing and degradation of plant items
How ageing mechanisms are identified for structures, systems and components, how degradation is monitored and mitigated, and how continued fitness for service is justified over the intended life.
It does not set inspection intervals or acceptance limits, and having an ageing management programme does not by itself justify life extension, which needs its own periodic safety review evidence.
UK51: management systems and quality management arrangements
How a licensee's management system, including its quality management arrangements, processes, document control, independent assurance and organisational learning, is judged to support nuclear safety.

Certification of a management system to a general quality standard is not the same as the nuclear management system expectations here, and the guide does not prescribe process structure or documentation format.
UK52: using probabilistic results and insights in decisions
How probabilistic safety analysis results and insights should and should not be used to inform design choices, operational decisions, risk-informed arguments and the demonstration of risk reduction.
It governs use of the results and does not set risk acceptance criteria; probabilistic insights do not substitute for the deterministic design basis or for the reasonable-practicability argument.
UK53: designing security into a facility from the outset

How security requirements are identified and embedded in design from the earliest stages so that protection is engineered in rather than added later, and how design decisions affecting security are recorded.
It addresses the design process for security and does not resolve conflicts between security features and safety functions on the same plant, which have to be argued in both cases.
UK54: security assessment of a generic new reactor design
How the security aspects of a generic reactor design are assessed alongside the safety assessment, what a requesting party is expected to submit, and how generic security claims are carried forward.
A generic security assessment is not a site security plan approval; site-specific threat, layout, response and personnel arrangements are outside it and are approved separately.
UK55: the environmental regulator's objective and principles for radioactive substances

What outcomes the environmental regulator is seeking when it permits radioactive substances activities, and what principles on optimisation, best available techniques, dose constraints and public confidence guide its decisions.
It states principles rather than permit conditions; it does not fix discharge limits for any site, and it does not determine what techniques count as best available for a given process.
UK56: generic developed principles used in environmental assessment of a design

What the environmental regulator expects a generic reactor design to demonstrate on radioactive substances management, radiological protection of people and the environment, site evaluation, engineering for environment protection and emergency preparedness.

These are principles for the generic environmental assessment and are not permit conditions; a design meeting them still needs a site-specific permit application with site data, and a withdrawn principle set does not transfer to a new topic area.
UK57: the environmental regulator's route through generic design assessment

How the environmental regulator, working with the nuclear regulator and the Welsh regulator, assesses a generic design, what environmental submissions a requesting party makes, and what a statement of design acceptability covers.
A statement of design acceptability is not an environmental permit and confers no right to discharge; site-specific limits, monitoring and best available techniques decisions all come later.
UK58: complying with a radioactive substances permit on a nuclear site

What a permit holder is expected to do about best available techniques, waste minimisation, discharge and disposal control, monitoring, record keeping, reporting and environmental management on a nuclear licensed site.
It explains how the environmental regulator expects permit obligations to be met but does not replace the conditions of a particular permit, and it does not deal with worker dose or nuclear safety.
UK59: releasing a nuclear site from radioactive substances regulation

What the environmental regulators expect a site operator to demonstrate about residual radioactivity, site characterisation, records and future use before the radioactive substances permit can be surrendered.

Release from radioactive substances regulation is separate from delicensing by the nuclear regulator; achieving one does not deliver the other, and the guidance does not set numerical release criteria for every situation.
UK60: requirements for authorising a geological disposal facility

What environmental safety case, site characterisation, design, operational and post-closure evidence the environmental regulators expect from an operator seeking authorisation to dispose of solid radioactive waste at depth.

It sets out what the environmental safety case has to address over very long timescales but does not settle site selection, does not fix waste acceptance criteria, and does not cover the nuclear site licensing of the surface facilities.
FI01: use of nuclear energy, licences and the waste obligation

The statute that makes the use of nuclear energy in Finland conditional on a chain of state decisions: a Government decision-in-principle ratified by Parliament, then a construction licence, then an operating licence, and it places the obligation to manage and fund the disposal of nuclear waste on the licence holder.

It carries almost no technical content: the safety requirements sit in STUK regulations and YVL guides, and a favourable decision-in-principle settles the political acceptability of a project, not its licensability.
FI02: contents of nuclear facility licence applications

Sets out what a licence application must contain and when, including the preliminary and final safety analysis reports, the quality management documentation, the security and emergency plans and the waste management plan, and it defines the role of STUK, the ministry and other authorities in the review.

It fixes the list and the timing of application documents but not the depth or the acceptable content of any of them; that is decided against the YVL guides, so a formally complete application can still be unreviewable.
FI03: radiation practices, justification and the safety licence system

The general radiation statute covering justification, optimisation and dose limitation for all exposure situations, the safety licence regime for radiation practices, and the duties of the radiation safety officer and of approved dosimetry services.

For a nuclear facility most operational radiation protection duties are enforced through the Nuclear Energy Act and the YVL C guides instead, and this Act does not itself state the numerical dose limits.
FI04: dose limits, reference levels and exemption in the radiation regime

Gives the effective and equivalent dose limits for workers, students and members of the public, the reference levels for existing and emergency exposure situations, and the general rules on exemption from regulatory control.
It constrains doses to people; it says nothing about the discharge limits for a particular site, which are set for the facility through the licence and the release monitoring guide.
FI05: binding safety regulation for a nuclear power plant

The legally binding regulation that carries the top-level safety objectives, the defence in depth structure, the release limits for postulated and severe accidents and the core damage frequency expectation, plus the duties on construction, commissioning, operation and decommissioning of a nuclear power plant.

It is written for a nuclear power plant: disposal facilities fall under a separate regulation, and it states goals and limits rather than any design solution that meets them, so a design cannot be measured against it without the YVL guides.
FI06: binding safety regulation for the disposal of nuclear waste
