FR10: carriage of dangerous goods on land, including class seven

The arrêté that makes ADR, RID and ADN applicable in France and adds national provisions: which derogations and additional conditions apply on French territory, the duties of the safety adviser, restrictions on routes and tunnels and the reporting obligations for road, rail and inland waterway carriage of radioactive material.

It governs carriage on public land routes only: package design approval, the security of nuclear material in transit and the internal movements inside an installation perimeter are each dealt with under separate texts.
FR11: protection and accountancy of nuclear material

The defence code regime for nuclear material outside the deterrent: the authorisation to hold, use, transfer or transport nuclear material, the obligation to account for it and to follow it physically, the physical protection duties and the inspection and sanction regime run by the ministry responsible for energy.

It is a separate authorisation from the installation création decree and answers to a different administration; the detailed protection requirements and the threat basis are not published, so the level of protection cannot be inferred from the code text.
FR12: physical protection of nuclear material while it is moving

The arrêté setting the protection and control requirements for nuclear material in transit: the approval regime for shipments, notification and escort arrangements, tracking and communication with the authorities and the conditions attached to stopping points.
It addresses malicious acts, not radiological safety of the package, and the operative annexes are not fully public, so a carrier cannot scope its obligations from the published text alone.
FR13: the merger that created the ASNR

The statute that reorganised nuclear safety and radiation protection governance by merging the former ASN with the technical support organisation IRSN into a single Autorité de sûreté nucléaire et de radioprotection, and that reassigns the powers, staff and expert functions accordingly.

It changes who issues and reviews, not what is required: existing ASN decisions, guides and RFS remain in force under the new issuer's name, so a reference list still carries the old ASN designations and has to be read that way.
FR14: acceleration of procedures for new reactors near existing sites

The statute easing and compressing the administrative route for new reactors built close to existing nuclear sites: derogations from planning and coastal law, an early-works regime before the création authorisation decree, and adjustments to the periodic review regime of existing reactors.

It shortens procedures without lowering the safety demonstration: the technical instruction against the general rules and the ASNR guides is unchanged, and its geographic and temporal scope is deliberately narrow, so it cannot be assumed to cover a greenfield site.
FR15: the required content of an installation safety report

The binding decision that fixes the structure and content of the rapport de sûreté for a basic nuclear installation at each stage — preliminary, provisional, final and updated — including the description of the installation, the hazard analyses, the demonstration of risk control, the operating rules and the interfaces with waste and emergency documents.

It settles what chapters exist and what must be addressed in them, not how deep the analysis has to go or which methods are acceptable, and a report that follows the structure can still be rejected on the substance of the demonstration.
FR16: fire risk control rules for basic nuclear installations

The binding decision on fire in a nuclear installation: the fire hazard analysis, sectorisation and its justification, control of combustible material and ignition sources, detection, fighting and confinement arrangements, the fire safety organisation and the interaction with the emergency plan.

It sets requirements rather than engineering rules: the resistance ratings, the extinguishing system design and the smoke and confinement calculations come from conventional standards and from the codes, and it does not settle how a fire-induced failure is postulated in the safety analysis.
FR17: control of nuisances and of environmental and health impact

The binding decision governing the environmental side of an installation: sampling and use of water, gaseous and liquid discharges and their authorisation limits, chemical and thermal nuisances, noise, environmental and radiological monitoring around the site, and the reporting of results to the regulator and the public.

It frames how limits are set and monitored; the numerical discharge limits themselves come in the individual authorisation decision for each site, and it does not cover the classical industrial permitting of installations on the site that fall outside the nuclear perimeter.
FR18: the waste management study and the waste inventory of an installation

The binding decision requiring each installation to produce and maintain an étude sur la gestion des déchets — waste minimisation at source, characterisation, the management route for each stream through to disposal or clearance — and an annual bilan of waste produced and held.

It requires a credible route to be described but cannot create one: where no authorised disposal route exists the study documents interim storage, and it does not settle the acceptance criteria of the destination facility, which are set by the disposal operator.
FR19: emergency preparedness duties and the internal emergency plan

The binding decision on how an operator prepares for and manages a radiological emergency: the emergency organisation and its activation, the content and testing of the plan d'urgence interne, on-site means and habitable premises, alerting the authorities, exercises and the return of experience after an event.

It covers the operator's on-site arrangements only; off-site protective action for the population is decided by the prefect under the plan particulier d'intervention, and the decision does not fix the accident sequences the plan has to be able to face.
FR20: seismic design of civil structures for nuclear installations

The regulator's accepted approach to designing civil works against the seismic input: how the design earthquake is turned into loads, soil-structure interaction, the analysis methods and damping assumptions, the treatment of concrete and steel structures and the interface with the equipment anchorage and the conventional structural codes.

It is one acceptable approach and not a mandatory method, it excludes long-term radioactive waste disposal structures, and it does not define the seismic hazard itself, which is derived separately for the site.
FR21: protection of nuclear installations against external flooding

The guide setting out how the flood hazard is characterised for a site — river, sea level, storm surge, rainfall, groundwater, dam or dyke failure and combinations of these — and how volumetric protection, drainage, watertightness and organisational measures are then justified.

It addresses flooding as an external hazard and stops there: internal flooding from pipe failures, the combination of flooding with other hazards beyond the cases it lists, and the plant modifications that a post-Fukushima hardened core requires are treated in separate documents.
FR22: design principles for pressurised water reactors

The regulator's expectations for the design of a new pressurised water reactor: the safety objectives and their link to defence in depth, the classification of systems and their functional criteria, the postulated initiating events and the acceptance criteria for each category, single failure and redundancy, design extension conditions and the practical elimination of situations with early or large releases.

It states design objectives and expectations, not the calculation methods or the qualified computer codes that demonstrate them, and it is written for a large water-cooled reactor, so its transposition to a small modular or non-water-cooled design is a judgement to be argued rather than assumed.
FR23: qualification of scientific computing tools used in the safety demonstration

The guide on what makes a calculation tool acceptable in a safety case: the definition of the domain of use, the verification of the equations and the numerics, the validation against experiment and against separate and integral effect tests, the uncertainty treatment, the user effect and the configuration control of the tool and its data.

It qualifies the tool for a stated domain, not the individual calculation: a qualified code used outside its validation domain, or with an unqualified user or unverified input deck, gives no more confidence than an unqualified one, and it does not accept any specific code by name.
FR24: treatment of departures from a defined requirement on a protection-important item

The guide on écarts de conformité: how to detect, characterise and record a departure of an élément important pour la protection from its exigence définie, how to judge the immediate acceptability of continued operation, the deadlines and the treatment plan, the generic extension to other installations and the interaction with the significant event declaration.

It structures the handling of an already identified departure; it does not tell an operator how to find them, does not fix the technical acceptability of operating with one, and does not replace the modification regime when the fix changes the installation.
FR25: risk-control policy and the operator's integrated management system

The guide on the top-level expectations of the arrêté INB in management terms: the written policy on control of risks and nuisances, the integrated management system covering safety, radiation protection, environment and security, the definition and surveillance of activités importantes pour la protection, competence, and the control of contractors and suppliers.

It describes what an acceptable management system addresses, not how it is organised: certification to a generic management standard does not answer the nuclear-specific duties on protection-important activities, and the guide does not settle the depth of surveillance owed to a given supplier.
FR26: transposing the WENRA reference levels onto operating reactors

The guide that maps the WENRA safety reference levels for existing reactors onto the French regulatory framework, showing which national text or practice answers each reference level and where additional expectations are placed on operating power reactors.

It is a mapping exercise for reactors already in operation: it does not create new requirements of its own, it does not apply to installations other than power reactors, and it does not settle how a gap identified against a reference level is to be closed.
FR27: final shutdown, decommissioning and delicensing of an installation

The guide covering the whole end-of-life route: the strategy and the choice of an immediate dismantling approach, the declaration of final shutdown, the content of the dossier supporting the decommissioning decree, the safety demonstration for dismantling operations, the end state and the conditions for déclassement from the list of basic nuclear installations.

It describes the regulatory route and the expected content, not the dismantling techniques or the dose and waste optimisation of a particular operation, and it does not settle the residual contamination criteria for site release, which are argued case by case.
FR28: clean-up of structures inside a nuclear installation

The guide on how the structures of an installation are decontaminated and how the result is demonstrated: the historical and radiological characterisation, the choice of clean-up methods, the sampling strategy and statistical treatment of measurements, and the documentation supporting a declaration that a structure has reached its target state.

It deals with structures and not with soils or with the site as a whole, and it does not fix a numerical release criterion: France has no generic clearance level for building structures, so the acceptable end state is negotiated on the basis of the intended future use.
FR29: management of soils contaminated by an installation's activities

The guide on contaminated ground within and around a nuclear installation: the historical study and characterisation strategy, the conceptual site model, the assessment of exposure through the future use of the land, remediation options and the memory and restrictions attached to residual contamination.

It handles the radiological component of soil contamination and defers chemical pollution to the classical contaminated land regime; it does not set a generic clean-up level, and it does not decide the servitudes or land-use restrictions, which are imposed by separate administrative acts.
FR30: establishing and changing the waste zoning plan of an installation

The guide on the plan de zonage déchets: how an installation is divided into zones producing waste that may be radioactive and zones producing conventional waste, the justification of each boundary, the controls at the interfaces and the procedure for changing a zone.

Zoning determines the presumed status of waste on production, not the actual radiological content of a given item, and a conventional zone classification does not exempt an operator from characterisation when the history of a room or a component gives reason to doubt it.
FR31: safety of deep geological disposal of radioactive waste

The guide setting out the regulator's expectations for a deep geological disposal facility: the safety functions expected of the host rock and the engineered barriers, the reversibility and retrievability requirement, the phased safety case across construction, operation and the post-closure period, and the treatment of long timescale uncertainty.

It states expectations for the safety case, not the acceptance criteria for individual waste packages nor the design of the facility, and it does not settle the specific technical choices of any project, which remain subject to the création authorisation instruction.
FR32: conformity assessment of the most demanding nuclear pressure equipment for reactors

The guide describing how the regulator expects the conformity assessment of the highest level of nuclear pressure equipment for pressurised water reactors to be carried out: material and manufacturing justification, the demonstration for equipment whose failure is not postulated, the qualification of manufacturing processes and non-destructive examination, and the documentation trail up to the conformity decision.

It explains an accepted route through the ESPN arrêté for a specific class of equipment and does not extend to other levels or to non-reactor installations; it is guidance, so a different route can be argued but has to be justified from first principles.
FR33: civil transport of radioactive substances on public roads

The guide describing how the regulator expects the modal transport rules to be applied by French consignors and carriers: package selection and approvals, the shipment approval and notification cases, contamination and dose rate checks before dispatch, documentation, and the interfaces with the operator's management system.

It restates and interprets the applicable transport rules rather than replacing them, and it does not cover the security of nuclear material in transit or the movements internal to an installation perimeter.
FR34: determination of seismic hazard for surface nuclear installations

The rule that defines the deterministic French approach to seismic hazard: the identification of seismotectonic zones and the historical earthquake catalogue, the derivation of the séisme maximal historiquement vraisemblable and of the séisme majoré de sécurité, and the resulting design ground motion and spectra for a surface installation.

It stops at the ground motion: the design of structures and equipment against it is treated by the ASN guide on seismic civil design and by the equipment codes, and it does not address seismically induced hazards such as landslide, liquefaction or upstream dam failure.
FR35: development and use of probabilistic safety assessment

The rule describing what the regulator expects of a probabilistic safety assessment for a pressurised water reactor: the scope and level of the study, the modelling of initiating events, systems and human actions, the data and uncertainty treatment, quality assurance of the study and the way results are used to support decisions.

It is a rule on how a study is built and used, not a set of numerical safety goals, and it does not make probabilistic results a substitute for the deterministic demonstration, which remains the primary basis of the French safety case.
FR36: design and operation of ventilation systems in non-reactor installations

The rule on dynamic containment in fuel cycle, research and waste installations: the cascade of pressures between zones, the filtration stages and their arrangement, redundancy and power supply of the extraction, monitoring of the ventilation function and the rules for its operation and testing.

It was written for installations other than reactors and reflects an older technical state; the arrêté INB and the installation-specific general operating rules now carry the binding obligations, so this rule is best treated as an indication of accepted practice rather than a current requirement set.
FR37: safety classification of mechanical, electrical and civil items

The rule that defines the historical French classification of mechanical equipment, electrical systems, structures and civil works by safety function, and the consequences of a class in terms of design rules, qualification and quality provisions.

It predates the arrêté INB and its vocabulary of éléments importants pour la protection and exigences définies, so it does not map one-to-one onto the current regulatory language, and it does not by itself determine which construction code applies to a given item.
FR38: mechanical design and construction rules for reactor nuclear islands

The French contractual code for mechanical equipment of a pressurised water reactor nuclear island: what design analysis rules, material procurement specifications, welding and fabrication provisions, examination methods and end-of-manufacturing documentation a supplier works to when a French-style mechanical scope is ordered.

It is a contract document rather than a regulation, so invoking it does not by itself discharge the nuclear pressure equipment conformity duties, and a regulator outside France decides case by case whether the code is an acceptable route.
FR39: in-service inspection and evaluation rules for reactor mechanical components

How mechanical equipment of a pressurised water reactor nuclear island is followed once in service: the in-service examination provisions, the qualification of non-destructive examination, the treatment of indications found, the evaluation of a detected flaw and the routes for repair or replacement.

It assumes the equipment was built to a compatible construction code, and it does not fix the plant-specific inspection scope or periodicity, which come from the operator's programme and from what the regulator demands at a periodic review.
FR40: design and construction rules for electrical and I&C equipment
Addresses the design, manufacture and qualification of electrical and I&C equipment for nuclear islands.
It sits alongside the international I&C standard series rather than replacing it, and acceptance of it outside its home jurisdiction is not automatic.
FR41: fuel assembly and core component design and manufacturing rules

The rules for designing, fabricating and inspecting fuel assemblies and the various core components of a pressurised water reactor, covering material specifications, manufacturing processes, dimensional control and acceptance examinations.
It covers how the assembly is made, not how the core behaves: neutronic design, thermal margins, criticality safety outside the reactor and the licensing of a fuel product sit entirely elsewhere.
FR42: mechanical rules for advanced, research and fusion reactor components

The mechanical design and construction code for components exposed to elevated temperature, creep and irradiation — advanced reactors, research reactors and fusion devices — covering design analysis for those regimes, material procurement, welding and joining techniques and examination.

It gives no answer for a water-cooled power reactor pressure boundary, and adopting it does not settle whether the operating conditions, materials and geometries of a novel design fall inside the domain the code actually covers.
FR43: civil works design and construction rules for reactor buildings

Rules for the civil engineering scope of a pressurised water reactor: geotechnical work, reinforced concrete structures, prestressed and metal containments, steel frames, anchors, embedded parts and containment leak testing.

It builds on the European structural codes rather than replacing them, and it does not set the hazard loads themselves — ground motion, flood level, aircraft and explosion loading come from the site studies and the regulator's guides.
FR44: civil works technical code issued for the EPR reactor line

The project-specific issue of the civil works rules prepared for the EPR, covering the same civil engineering scope for that reactor line and reflecting the assumptions made when that design was assessed.

It is tied to one reactor line and to the national annexes assumed when it was drawn up, so citing it elsewhere does not carry over the regulatory acceptance the design once obtained in a particular country.
FR45: fire protection design and construction rules for the EPR reactor line

How fire protection systems are designed, built and installed to manage the fire hazard in a pressurised water reactor: general provisions, safety design principles, fire protection design bases, construction provisions and installation rules for the components and equipment.

It addresses the protection systems and not the fire hazard analysis that justifies the sectorisation or the failure assumptions, and the binding French fire requirements for a nuclear installation come from a regulator's decision rather than from the code.
AS01: The statute that governed Indian nuclear activity for six decades, including state monopoly on fissile material and the delegation under which the regulator acted.
It has been replaced. A 2025 statute recast the framework, opened ownership and gave the regulator statutory standing, so anything resting on the older delegation has to be re-checked.
AS02: notified rules on radiation protection and the control of radiation sources

The binding national rules on dose control and optimisation, the duties of the employer and of the radiological safety officer, licensing and registration of radiation sources and installations, and the disposal of radioactive waste under the parent Act.

They set legal duties and the consenting framework but not the shielding, layout or ventilation design that delivers them, and the reactor licensing route runs separately through the AERB consenting process rather than through these rules alone.
AS03: factory and occupational safety law inside atomic energy installations

Applies conventional factory law — health, welfare, hours, hazardous processes, dangerous machinery, occupational hygiene and notification of accidents — to factories within Department of Atomic Energy units, with AERB acting as the competent authority in place of the state factory inspectorate.

It governs industrial and occupational safety only; conformity with it says nothing about radiological safety, which is dealt with under the Radiation Protection Rules and the AERB codes, and the two inspection regimes have different triggers and reporting lines.
AS04: civil liability for nuclear damage act
The statute that established operator liability for nuclear damage in India, including the supplier right of recourse that shaped every supply contract negotiated under it.

It has been replaced by the 2025 statute, which recasts both the liability cap and the recourse provision, so contracts and risk assessments written against the older text no longer describe the position.
AS05: AERB safety code for site evaluation of nuclear facilities

The mandatory Indian requirements for evaluating a site: grounds on which a site is rejected outright, the natural and human-induced external events to be characterised, population distribution and the feasibility of emergency arrangements, and the site-related design basis handed on to the designer.

It does not give the investigation methods or acceptance criteria for individual hazards, which sit in the siting safety guides, and site acceptance under it does not deliver the environmental clearance, which is a separate consent from the environment ministry.
AS06: AERB safety guide on seismic studies and design basis ground motion
How the geological, seismological and geotechnical investigation of an Indian nuclear power plant site is to be carried out, and how the design basis ground motion is derived from it.

It stops at the free-field ground motion; structural response, seismic categorisation and equipment qualification come from the design guides, and it does not deal with seismically induced flooding, liquefaction remediation or slope failure as design problems.
AS07: AERB safety guide on atmospheric dispersion and modelling for nuclear sites
The meteorological measurement programme expected at a site and the dispersion modelling used to estimate the transport and dilution of routine and accidental atmospheric releases.

It supports dose estimation but sets neither the dose criteria nor the source term, and the models it describes are only as good as the site-specific measurement campaign they depend on, which cannot be substituted by regional data.
AS08: AERB safety code for the design of pressurised heavy water reactor plants

The mandatory design requirements for Indian PHWR nuclear power plants: defence in depth, safety functions and their classification, design basis events, the two diverse and independent shutdown systems, containment, and the qualification of items important to safety.

It is written around the PHWR line and is not a design code for light water or advanced reactors; it states requirements rather than accepted methods, and it contains none of the mechanical or civil construction rules that give effect to them.
AS09: AERB safety code for the design of light water reactor plants

The Indian design safety requirements applied to light water reactor nuclear power plants, including imported designs, covering safety functions and classification, design basis events, engineered safety features and containment.

It does not resolve the reconciliation between an imported vendor's home code set and Indian requirements, which is settled case by case during consenting review, and it leaves the PHWR-specific provisions to the separate PHWR code.
AS10: AERB safety guide on safety classification and seismic categorisation

How structures, systems and components of a PHWR plant are assigned to safety classes and seismic categories, and what those assignments imply for the design codes, manufacturing rules and quality measures applied to each item.

The classification drives which code applies but the guide does not contain those codes, and it does not settle the classification of computer-based functions or of equipment credited only in severe accident management.
AS11: AERB safety guide on safety systems for pressurised heavy water reactors

Design expectations for the engineered safety systems of a PHWR — shutdown systems, emergency core cooling, containment isolation and decay heat removal — including redundancy, physical and functional separation, testability and the single failure treatment.
It does not carry out the safety analysis that shows the systems perform their function, and it does not cover the non-safety systems and portable equipment credited in design extension conditions.
AS12: AERB safety guide on radiation protection aspects in plant design

How radiation protection is built into a PHWR plant by design: layout and zoning, shielding, ventilation and containment of airborne activity, access control, decontamination provisions and the design measures that limit collective dose during maintenance.

It addresses design provisions only, not the operational radiation protection programme, the dose limits or the work planning, which come from the Radiation Protection Rules and the radiation protection code.
AS13: AERB safety guide on safety related instrumentation and control

Design expectations for reactor protection, safety actuation and safety-related monitoring in a PHWR plant, including independence and separation, testability and surveillance, and the treatment of common cause failure between redundant channels.

It does not by itself carry the software development, verification and qualification lifecycle for computer-based safety systems, and the classification of I&C functions that decides how far it bites comes from the classification guide.
AS14: AERB safety guide on containment system design

How the containment of a PHWR plant is designed and qualified: pressure capability and leak-tightness, isolation of penetrations, energy management and the associated proof and periodic leak testing regime.
It does not supply the civil design code for the containment structure, nor the hydrogen management and late-phase severe accident loads that lie beyond the design basis it addresses.
AS15: AERB safety code for nuclear power plant operation

The mandatory requirements on the operating organisation: management structure and staffing, authorisation of operating personnel, technical specifications and operating limits, maintenance, surveillance and testing, control of modifications, event reporting and on-site emergency arrangements.
It sets what the operator has to have in place but not the plant-specific operating limits and conditions themselves, which are derived from the safety analysis and approved separately by AERB.
AS16: AERB safety guide on in-service inspection of nuclear power plants

The scope, methods, intervals, personnel qualification and reporting for in-service inspection of pressure-retaining components and other items important to safety in an operating Indian nuclear power plant.

It does not provide flaw acceptance or fitness-for-service evaluation rules, nor the wider ageing management programme, and the inspection access designed into the plant years earlier limits what it can later require.
AS17: AERB safety guide on periodic safety review of nuclear power plants

How the periodic reassessment of an operating Indian plant against current standards and operating experience is scoped, performed and reported, and how the resulting safety improvements are prioritised and tracked.
It does not by itself authorise continued or long-term operation, and it contains none of the ageing management, equipment qualification or reanalysis methods on which its conclusions actually rest.
AS18: AERB safety code for quality assurance in nuclear power plants

The mandatory requirements for establishing and implementing a quality assurance programme across siting, design, construction, commissioning, operation and decommissioning, including the responsibilities retained by the utility when work is placed with suppliers.

It is a programme requirement and not a certified management system standard; it does not itself set the graded quality measures for a particular item, which follow from the safety classification of that item.
AS19: AERB safety guide on establishing and implementing the quality assurance programme

How a utility is expected to set up, document and run the quality assurance programme required by the quality assurance code: organisation and interfaces, procedures, document and record control, control of purchased items and services, and internal audit.

It does not go into supplier surveillance and vendor qualification at the depth a first-of-a-kind supply chain needs, and having the programme documented is not the same as the independent assessment of how well it is being implemented.
AS20: AERB safety code for radiation protection at nuclear facilities

The mandatory radiation protection requirements for Indian nuclear facilities: the protection programme and the responsibilities within it, classification and zoning of areas, workplace and personnel monitoring, control of internal and external exposure, and the handling of planned special exposures.
It gives no shielding design methods, and it does not carry the environmental discharge authorisation, which is handled through separate approvals and through the waste management code.
AS21: AERB guidance on criteria for planning, preparedness and response to nuclear or radiological emergency

The intervention criteria, emergency classes, planning zones and response arrangements used in India for nuclear and radiological emergencies, and how the operator, the district administration and the state relate to each other during a response.

It does not write the site emergency plan, and the off-site plan it presupposes is the responsibility of the district administration, whose readiness the operator does not control but does depend upon.
AS22: AERB safety code for the management of radioactive waste

The mandatory requirements covering generation, segregation, characterisation, handling, treatment, conditioning, storage, transport and disposal of radioactive waste, and the authorisation of waste management facilities.

It does not fix the clearance or exemption levels applied to a particular consignment leaving regulatory control, and it does not settle the disposal route for long-lived and high level waste in India, which remains a policy question.
AS23: AERB safety guide on near surface disposal of radioactive waste
Siting, design, operation, closure and post-closure institutional control expectations for near surface disposal facilities receiving low and intermediate level radioactive waste.

It does not cover deep geological disposal or long-lived and high level waste, and it does not set the waste acceptance criteria for a given facility, which are derived from that facility's own safety assessment.
AS24: AERB safety guide on decommissioning of nuclear facilities

How decommissioning of Indian nuclear power plants and research reactors is planned and carried out, from the preliminary plan required while the plant is still being designed, through characterisation, dismantling and waste routes, to the final radiological survey.

It does not fix the end state or the clearance criteria for release of the site and of materials, which are decided case by case, and the financial provision for decommissioning is settled outside it.
AS25: AERB safety code for the safe transport of radioactive material

The Indian transport regime: classification and activity limits, package types with their design and test requirements, contamination and external radiation control, marking, labelling and documentation, and the competent authority approvals for package designs and shipments.

It does not replace the modal rules of the road, rail, air and maritime authorities that also govern the movement, and approval of a package design under it says nothing about the physical protection arrangements required for the consignment.
AS26: AERB safety guide on the consenting process for power and research reactors

The stages of Indian regulatory consent — siting, construction, commissioning in steps, operation and decommissioning — the submissions expected at each stage, and the multi-tier committee review through which AERB grants them.

It describes process and deliverables rather than the technical acceptance criteria applied at each stage, and it does not cover the environmental, coastal and land clearances that run in parallel on their own timetables.
AS27: AERB safety guide on regulatory review of level one probabilistic safety assessment

The methodology AERB applies when reviewing a level one PSA for a nuclear power plant or research reactor: scope and boundary conditions, modelling assumptions, data and dependency treatment, quantification, and the form of the review report.

It is a review guide rather than a PSA standard, so it does not tell the analyst how to build the model, and it does not extend to level two or level three assessment or to risk-informed decision making.
AS28: AERB safety guide on the format and content of the safety analysis report
The expected structure and chapter-by-chapter content of the safety analysis report submitted to AERB for a nuclear power plant, and the level of detail expected in each part.

Following the format does not make the safety case adequate: the analysis methods, computer codes and acceptance criteria come from elsewhere, and the depth expected differs sharply between the preliminary and the final report.
AS29: AERB guidelines for uranium oxide fuel fabrication facilities

The radiological and industrial safety expectations for uranium oxide fuel fabrication plants: layout and confinement, criticality control, contamination and airborne activity control, effluent and waste handling, and emergency arrangements.

It does not extend to mixed oxide or other plutonium-bearing fuel fabrication, and it does not contain the criticality safety analysis methods and validated data on which the plant layout and batch limits actually depend.
AS30: AERB safety guide on the security of radioactive sources

The security arrangements expected for radioactive sources held in Indian radiation facilities, graded by source category, covering access control, detection and delay, response arrangements, source accounting and control during transfer.

It deals with sources in radiation facilities, not with the physical protection of nuclear material and nuclear installations, which is governed by separate and largely non-public arrangements that no open document in this register describes.
AS31: The statute behind Japanese nuclear licensing: it governs the permission to install reactors and to handle nuclear source and fuel material, the design and construction approval steps, operating restrictions, inspection, and the powers of the Nuclear Regulation Authority.

This register names the Act only. The authoritative text is Japanese and the English rendering is an unofficial translation; the cabinet orders and NRA ordinances that carry most of the enforceable detail are not listed here.
AS32: the NRA new regulatory requirements framework

The post-Fukushima package of requirements the NRA applies when screening Japanese reactors: strengthened external event provisions including earthquake, tsunami and volcanic hazard, internal hazards, and mandatory measures against severe accidents and intentional aircraft impact.

Only the framework is named here. The binding requirements are written in Japanese in NRA ordinances and interpretation documents; the English outlines the NRA publishes are summaries and not the regulatory text, and individual requirements are not reproduced in this register.
AS33: the NRA ordinance on standards for the siting, structure and equipment of commercial reactors
The ordinance that carries the design-side regulatory requirements for commercial power reactors and their auxiliary facilities, against which an installation permit application is judged.

This register names the ordinance but not the interpretation documents and review guides that decide how each clause is read in practice, and the authoritative wording is Japanese with no official English version.
AS34: NRA review guides used in reactor screening
The body of guidance the NRA uses when reviewing applications, covering matters such as seismic and tsunami design basis, internal and external hazards, safety analysis and severe accident measures.

Only the family is named here. The individual guides are issued in Japanese, are not consolidated into a numbered series with official English equivalents, and this register deliberately does not attempt to identify them one by one.
AS35: The Japanese Society of Mechanical Engineers code family for nuclear power generation facilities, which answers how nuclear mechanical components are designed, constructed and later assessed for continued service.

Only the code family is named here. The individual codes are sold, are published in Japanese, and whether a given code may be used depends on regulatory endorsement of that specific code, which this register does not track.
AS36: the JEAC and JEAG code and guide family

The nuclear codes and guides of the Japan Electric Association's nuclear standards committee, addressing questions such as the management system for safety, seismic design, fire protection, digital safety systems, fuel management and maintenance management.

Only the family is named here. Individual documents are sold by the association in Japanese, and endorsement of any one of them by the regulator is decided separately and is not recorded in this register.
AS37: The national statute that sets the safety responsibilities of licensees, the licensing and oversight powers of the regulator, requirements on siting, operation, waste and emergency response, information disclosure and public participation, and the penalties regime.

This register names the law only. The authoritative text is Chinese and English versions are unofficial; the administrative regulations, departmental rules and provincial arrangements through which the law actually bites are not listed here.
AS38: the HAF series of Chinese nuclear safety regulations

The binding regulation series issued by the national nuclear safety authority, covering matters such as siting, design, operation and quality assurance of nuclear installations, and the regulatory control of nuclear material and radiation sources.

Only the series is named here. Individual HAF documents are not identified, the authoritative text is Chinese, and any English version circulating is an unofficial translation whose numbering may not match the current issue.
AS39: the HAD series of Chinese nuclear safety guides
The guidance series that elaborates how the requirements in the HAF regulations are expected to be met, organised in families that follow the regulation they support.
Only the series is named here. Individual HAD documents are not listed and the authoritative text is Chinese, so the mapping from a HAD number to a subject cannot be relied on from this register.
AS40: Chinese national standards applied to nuclear facilities

The national standard families used alongside the nuclear safety regulations, answering questions of basic radiation protection, civil and structural design, testing and measurement, and general engineering practice as applied on Chinese nuclear sites.
Only the family is named here. Individual standards are sold, the authoritative text is Chinese, and this register does not record which standards a particular reactor design was licensed against.
AS41: the Chinese nuclear energy industry standard family
The energy sector standard family covering nuclear island equipment and materials, manufacturing, examination and related engineering practice for nuclear power plants.

Only the family is named here. Individual standards are sold in Chinese, and whether a given standard is contractually binding on a project follows from the contract and the licensing basis rather than from anything stated in this register.
AS42: The statute governing the licensing of nuclear reactors and related facilities in the Republic of Korea, the duties of licensees, inspection and enforcement, radiation protection, and the powers of the Nuclear Safety and Security Commission.

This register names the Act only. The authoritative text is Korean and the published English version is an unofficial translation; the Enforcement Decree, Enforcement Regulation and Commission notices that carry the technical detail are treated separately or not at all.
AS43: the enforcement decree and enforcement regulation under the Korean act

The subordinate instruments that turn the Nuclear Safety Act into operable requirements: application contents, licensing procedures, inspection regimes, technical standards for facilities and equipment, and radiation dose control.
Only the instruments are named. Their content is Korean and translations are unofficial, and this register does not identify which articles bear on any particular facility type or lifecycle stage.
AS44: notices of the Korean nuclear safety and security commission

The numbered notices through which the Commission issues detailed technical requirements — safety analysis, radiation protection, quality assurance, accident management, security and reporting — that supplement the Act and its subordinate rules.

Only the family of notices is named here. Individual notices are numbered and issued in Korean, are amended frequently, and are not listed one by one in this register, so the numbering seen in a project document should be checked against the current Korean source.
AS45: The technical guidance the Korean safety institute uses in its reviews and inspections, setting out acceptable methods for demonstrating conformity with the Commission's requirements.

Only the family is named here. Individual guides are published in Korean and their designations are not reproduced in this register, and they are review guidance rather than binding requirements in their own right.
AS46: the Russian federal law on the use of atomic energy

The framework statute for the Russian regime: it defines nuclear installations and facilities, the operating organisation and its responsibilities, licensing and state oversight, physical protection, and liability for nuclear damage.

This register names the law only. The authoritative text is Russian and English translations are unofficial; the government decrees and the regulator's own instruments through which licensing actually operates are not enumerated here.
AS47: the NP series of Russian federal norms and rules

The binding federal norms and rules in the field of the use of atomic energy, covering safety of nuclear installations, fuel cycle facilities, research reactors, radiation sources, waste management, transport and physical protection.

Only the series is named here. Individual NP documents are not listed, the authoritative text is Russian with no official English version, and the series spans facility types whose documents differ substantially from one another.
AS48: general safety provisions for nuclear power plants

The top-level Russian safety requirements document for nuclear power plants: safety functions and the classification of systems, defence in depth, design basis and beyond design basis conditions, single failure treatment, and the responsibilities of the operating organisation.

The authoritative text is Russian and no official English version exists. This register names the document without reproducing its classification scheme or its accident category definitions, which do not map cleanly onto Western terminology.
AS49: the PNAE strength and welding code family
The Russian code family that answers how equipment and piping of nuclear power installations are dimensioned for strength, and how welded joints and cladding are made, examined and accepted.

Only the family is named here. Individual documents are sold in Russian, some parts have been superseded or overlaid by newer federal norms, and this register does not record which parts remain in force for a given plant.
AS50: the Canadian nuclear safety and control act

The statute that establishes the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, prohibits nuclear activity except under licence, and provides the powers to licence, certify, inspect, order and enforce across the whole nuclear sector.

Canada is carried here at framework level only. The Act is named without the regulations and without the licence conditions handbook, which is where a specific licensee's obligations are actually pinned down.
AS51: regulations made under the Canadian act

The family of regulations that give effect to the Act, covering general safety and control, Class I nuclear facilities, radiation protection, nuclear security, packaging and transport of nuclear substances, and cost recovery.

Only the family is named here. The individual regulations are not listed, and the licence conditions handbook that binds a particular licensee is issued case by case and forms no part of this register.
AS52: the CNSC regulated facilities and activities document series

The first REGDOC series, organised by the kind of facility or activity being licensed — reactor facilities, Class IB facilities, uranium mines and mills, Class II facilities, prescribed equipment certification, and nuclear substances and radiation devices — and giving the licence application expectations for each.
Only the series and its themes are named here. Individual REGDOC numbers within the series are not listed, and a REGDOC becomes binding on a licensee only where it is referenced in that licence.
AS53: the CNSC safety and control areas document series

The second REGDOC series, structured on the safety and control areas: management system, human performance management, operating performance, safety analysis, physical design, fitness for service, radiation protection, conventional health and safety, environmental protection, emergency management and fire protection, waste management, security, safeguards and non-proliferation, and packaging and transport.

Only the series and its themes are named here. The individual documents within each theme are not listed, several are versioned, and applicability to a given licensee follows from the licence and its conditions handbook rather than from the series structure.
AS54: the CNSC other regulatory areas document series

The third REGDOC series, covering reporting requirements, public and Indigenous engagement, financial guarantees, Commission proceedings, the Commission's own processes and practices, and the glossary of regulatory terminology.

Only the series and its themes are named here. Individual documents are not listed, and the engagement and financial guarantee expectations for a specific project are settled in the licensing process rather than fixed by the series.
AS55: the pre-licensing vendor design review process

How a reactor vendor can obtain an early, optional CNSC opinion on whether a design intent meets Canadian requirements, what the review phases look at, and what the vendor has to submit to enter them.

A vendor design review is not a licence, a certification or a design approval, and this register names the process document without the phase-specific expectations and focus areas that are agreed for each individual review.
EX01: supervision and control of shipments of radioactive waste and spent fuel
Sets the authorisation and consent procedure for moving radioactive waste and spent fuel between member states and into or out of the Union.
It is a shipment consent regime. It says nothing about the acceptability of the waste at its destination.
EX02: maximum permitted levels of radioactive contamination of food and feed
Fixes the levels that become applicable to food and feed after a nuclear accident, and the mechanism by which they are activated.
The levels are dormant until the Commission activates them, so they are an emergency instrument rather than an operating limit.
EX03: shipments of radioactive substances between member states
Requires prior declaration to the competent authorities of the receiving state for shipments of sealed sources and radioactive waste within the Union.
It sits alongside the transport safety regime and does not replace package approval.
EX04: radioactive substances in water intended for human consumption
Sets the monitoring obligations and parametric values for radioactivity in drinking water.
It applies to the water supply, not to the discharge, and the two are regulated by different authorities.
EX05: Obliges member states to maintain facilities for monitoring radioactivity in air, water and soil, and gives the Commission a right of access to verify them.
It creates a state obligation and a Commission verification power, not a licensee reporting duty.
EX06: application of Article 37 of the Euratom Treaty
Sets out what general data on the disposal of radioactive waste has to be submitted to the Commission, for which categories of facility, and when in the project.
The submission has to precede the national authorisation of discharges, which puts it early and on its own timetable.
EX07: Recommends a common format and content for reporting airborne and liquid discharges from nuclear power reactors and reprocessing plants.
It standardises reporting. Discharge limits themselves are national.
EX08: A recurring peer review across the Union on a chosen topic, such as ageing management or fire protection, resulting in national action plans.
It is a peer review of the national regime and the operators in it, not a licensing step, but its findings tend to reappear as regulatory expectations.
EX09: A common approach among European radiation protection and nuclear safety regulators to aligning protective action strategies across borders.
It is a voluntary alignment between authorities. It does not change any national emergency plan by itself.
EX10: sustainable finance criteria for nuclear activities
Sets the conditions under which nuclear generation, new build and life extension count as sustainable activities, including requirements on fuel, waste routes and decommissioning funds.
It is a financing instrument, not a safety instrument, but the conditions it sets are checked by auditors and can constrain a project independently of the regulator.
EX11: The German statutory basis for licensing, oversight, waste and decommissioning of nuclear installations, including the framework for financing.
The Act sets the frame; the substance sits in the ordinances, the safety requirements and the KTA rules beneath it.
EX12: The German transposition of the radiation protection regime, covering exposure situations, authorisation, clearance and emergency response.
Clearance and exemption routes are detailed and procedural, and they differ from those of neighbouring states.
EX13: safety requirements for nuclear power plants
The German safety requirements for power reactors together with the interpretation documents that give them practical meaning.
They were written around the operating German fleet and the fleet has been shut down, so their maintenance and their applicability to a new design both need checking.
EX14: reactor safety and waste management commission recommendations
Recommendations of the German advisory commissions on reactor safety and on waste management, used as the technical reasoning behind regulatory positions.
They are advisory. They bind nobody, and several predate the current requirement framework.
US66: An optional third licensing framework in the United States, written so that the requirements follow from the risk a design actually presents rather than from light water reactor architecture.
It is optional and new, so there is little precedent for how it is applied in practice, and choosing it commits a project to a body of guidance that is still being built out.
AS56: statute governing nuclear energy for peaceful purposes

The Indian statute that replaced both the atomic energy legislation and the civil nuclear liability legislation: it opens participation beyond state entities, gives the regulator statutory standing, and recasts the liability and recourse regime.
It is recent, so the subordinate rules and the regulator’s reissued codes that give it practical effect are still appearing, and the older codes remain in circulation.
PLN01: The statutory basis for nuclear and radiation safety regulation in Poland. It establishes the licensing and supervision framework, the competent nuclear regulatory authority and the principal duties governing nuclear activities.

Use the consolidated official Polish text and the implementing regulations for project decisions. This register is an orientation aid and does not determine which provision applies to a particular licence.
PLN02: Sets the site-assessment criteria, exclusion factors and the required content of the site report for a nuclear facility in Poland.
The regulation is site- and licensing-specific. It does not replace project geotechnical, seismic, flooding, environmental or external-hazard analyses required by the authority.
PLN03: Polish safety-analysis and preliminary safety-report requirements
Defines the scope and manner of safety analyses and the required content of the preliminary safety report submitted for a Polish nuclear facility.
It specifies the regulatory safety-case framework; it is not itself a calculation method and does not prescribe a single analysis code or modelling tool.
PLN04: Sets nuclear-safety and radiological-protection requirements that the design of a Polish nuclear facility must take into account, including defence in depth and design provisions for safety functions and hazards.

Detailed applicability depends on the facility, licence basis and decisions of the competent authority. International codes and standards do not become Polish legal requirements merely because the project uses them.
PLN05: Sets nuclear-safety and radiological-protection requirements for commissioning and operation of nuclear facilities in Poland.
This is an operational regulatory layer. Plant-specific licence conditions, procedures and later amendments remain controlling and must be checked against the current official legal text.
PLN06: Sets nuclear-safety and radiological-protection requirements for decommissioning nuclear facilities and the required content of the decommissioning report.
The regulation does not select a decommissioning strategy or demonstrate release criteria for a specific site; those remain project- and licence-specific.
PLN07: Safety-important activities at a Polish nuclear power plant

Defines activities of particular importance to nuclear safety and radiological protection and the competence framework for personnel carrying them out during commissioning, operation or decommissioning.
It is a personnel and organisational control layer, not a substitute for the plant's management system, operating limits or licence conditions.
PLN08: Periodic nuclear safety assessment in Poland
Defines the periodic safety assessment framework for a nuclear facility and the review material that supports continued operation and long-term operation decisions.
The regulation establishes the review obligation and structure; it does not predetermine the outcome or replace detailed ageing, deterministic and probabilistic analyses.
PLN09: Physical protection of nuclear materials and facilities in Poland
Sets the national physical-protection framework for nuclear material and nuclear facilities.
Security-sensitive implementation details and plant-specific arrangements are not reproduced here; applicability and safeguards/security interfaces must be checked with the competent authorities.
PLN10: Radioactive waste and spent nuclear fuel requirements in Poland
Sets requirements for classification, handling, storage and management of radioactive waste and spent nuclear fuel within the Polish Atomic Law framework.
Facility-specific waste acceptance criteria, package specifications and disposal-route conditions remain outside this orientation record.
PLN11: Documents required for Polish nuclear licensing applications
Specifies the documents required with applications or notifications for activities involving ionising-radiation exposure, including the nuclear-facility licensing documentation layer.
The document list is a regulatory filing framework; satisfying the list does not by itself demonstrate the adequacy of the underlying safety case.
PLN12: Sets the scope of hazard analysis and the form in which conclusions from that analysis are presented for regulated activities involving ionising radiation.
It is a regulatory analysis framework, not a prescribed accident-analysis code and not a replacement for nuclear-facility safety analyses required by other regulations.
PLN13: Emergency planning for radiation events in Poland
Sets requirements for emergency plans for radiation events and the organisation of preparedness and response.
A plant-specific emergency plan, off-site arrangements and operational intervention criteria must be checked against the current licence basis and competent-authority arrangements.
PLN14: Environmental radiation monitoring programmes in Poland
Defines the scope of environmental radiation monitoring programmes for organisations classified in hazard categories I or II.
It is a monitoring-programme requirement; it does not set a plant-specific discharge authorisation or replace environmental permitting.
PLN15: Funding final spent-fuel, waste and decommissioning costs
Sets the payment mechanism used to cover final management of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste and decommissioning costs for a nuclear power plant.
This is a financing obligation. It does not establish technical waste acceptance, decommissioning or safety requirements.

S01: Establishes the site ground motion hazard, including the seismotectonic model, source characterisation and the hazard curves.
It does not give the design input directly. The design ground motion is derived from it by a separate, regulated step.
S02: Establishes soil profile, dynamic soil properties, liquefaction potential and foundation conditions.
It does not size the foundation.
S03: Establishes the flooding hazard from river, sea, precipitation, snowmelt, dam failure and combinations of these.
It does not decide the platform level.
S04: Establishes temperature, wind, tornado, precipitation, snow, lightning and drought parameters for the site.
Combination rules with other hazards sit in the design basis, not here.
S05: Screens and quantifies aircraft crash, explosion, toxic release, pipeline, transport and industrial hazards around the site.
Screening out a hazard is a judgement the regulator will re-examine.
S06: Population distribution and emergency planning feasibility
Establishes the population, land use and infrastructure around the site and whether protective actions are feasible.
It does not fix the planning zone sizes, which are set nationally.
S07: Establishes the pre-operational radiological state of the environment against which future impact is measured.
It must be done before operation. Afterwards it cannot be reconstructed.
S08: Assesses the effects of the project on the environment, including radiological and non-radiological effects and, where triggered, transboundary effects.
It is a consent procedure, not a safety assessment, and it runs on its own statutory timetable.
S09: Cooling water and thermal discharge study
Establishes water availability, intake and discharge design and the thermal and chemical effect on the receiving water.
Abstraction and discharge limits are set by permit, not by the study.
S10: Establishes whether the grid can accept the unit and whether it can supply the plant reliably, including loss of off-site power frequency.
Grid weakness is a safety input, and it belongs in the design basis rather than only in the connection agreement.
S11: The central licensing document: the design basis, the analysis, the classification and the operational limits, presented as one argument.
Its structure is set by the national regime. There is no international format.
S12: Demonstrates that acceptance criteria are met for the postulated initiating events across the plant states.
It does not cover multiple failure and severe accident sequences unless they are explicitly included.
S13: Quantifies accident sequence frequencies and release categories, and identifies the dominant contributors.
Numbers depend on scope and assumptions. A comparison between two PSAs is rarely meaningful.
S14: Demonstrates subcriticality for all credible normal and abnormal conditions in fissile material operations.
Validation of the calculation route against representative critical experiments is part of the assessment, not an optional extra.
S15: Source term and radiological consequence analysis
Establishes the release to the environment for the analysed conditions and the resulting doses.
It underpins both the safety case and the emergency plan, which use it differently.
S16: Establishes shielding, zoning and the expected collective and individual doses of the workforce.
Optimisation is a design duty, not a check performed at the end.
S17: Establishes fire compartments, fire loads, safe shutdown paths and the protection measures for each area.
It has to be reconciled with the internal hazard analysis and with the cable routing, which are usually done by other teams.
S18: Establishes that safety-classified equipment performs its function under the environmental, seismic and ageing conditions it will see.
Qualification is item-specific and it expires. A certificate is not qualification.
S19: Identifies ageing mechanisms for passive and active items and sets the monitoring and replacement programme.
It is the core of any lifetime extension case and takes years of data to build.
S20: Establishes task analysis, control room design, staffing and the human reliability input to the safety analysis.
It cannot be added at the end. Late human factors findings mean rework of the interface.
S21: Establishes waste streams, volumes, categories, treatment routes, storage and the route to disposal or clearance.
Waste acceptance criteria come from the destination facility, which may not exist yet.
S22: Establishes the decommissioning concept, the end state, the waste implications and the cost and funding basis.
An initial plan is required from the design stage in most regimes, long before it is used.
S23: Establishes the on-site and off-site emergency arrangements, the planning zones and the interfaces with public authorities.
Off-site arrangements are not the licensee's to decide alone.
S24: Establishes the physical protection design and the response to the design basis threat.
The threat basis is state-supplied and not public. This work cannot be done in the open.
S25: Safeguards design information and safeguards by design
Establishes the design information to be declared, the material balance areas and the measures that make verification practicable.
Late safeguards input can force physical changes to a built facility.
S26: Establishes the package design, its compliance with the transport regime and the route and logistics assumptions.
Approval of a package design and approval of a shipment are separate acts.
S27: Establishes that the analysis codes are applicable and validated for the phenomena and the plant being analysed, including any separate-effect and integral test programme.
For a first-of-a-kind design this is often the longest item on the critical path and it is routinely underestimated.
S28: Re-examines the whole safety case against current standards, cumulative ageing and operating experience.
It is not an audit. It regularly produces modification programmes.
S29: Establishes the staged test programme with acceptance criteria and hold points, from pre-operational testing through fuel load to power ascension.
Test results are part of the licensing evidence, not an internal record.
S30: Site characterisation for release from regulatory control
Establishes the residual contamination and demonstrates that the end state criteria are met.
Release criteria are national and vary widely. The end state has to be agreed before the work, not after.

B01: The safety case in full: design basis, analysis, classification, operating limits, management arrangements, and the justification for every departure from expected guidance.
B02: Dose assessments, the optimisation argument, monitoring arrangements, worker classification and the discharge authorisation basis.
B03: The environmental impact assessment, discharge and abstraction permits, waste routes, and the monitoring programme.
B04: Abstraction volumes, thermal and chemical discharge, effects on the receiving water and on other users.
B05: Land use consent, construction traffic and logistics, local infrastructure, and the local element of emergency arrangements.
B06: Connection studies, grid code compliance, plant behaviour on grid disturbance, and the reliability of off-site power.
B07: Flight path data, obstacle clearance, and the input to the accidental aircraft crash assessment.
B08: Design information at an early stage and updated through construction, accountancy reports, and access for verification.
B09: Basic technical characteristics, accountancy and reporting under the Euratom regulation, in parallel with IAEA obligations.
B10: General data on radioactive discharges before authorisation under Article 37, and notification of the investment project.
B11: The physical protection plan against the national design basis threat, personnel vetting arrangements and response coordination.
B12: Independent re-analysis, method review and confirmatory calculations on behalf of the regulator. In practice this is where technical arguments are actually contested.
B13: Evidence of the liability regime, financial security, and the risk basis for cover.
B14: End-use assurances, licences for controlled items and technology, and the intergovernmental agreements behind them.
B15: Waste stream declarations, conformity with waste acceptance criteria, packaging and transfer schedules.
B16: Off-site emergency arrangements, alerting, protective action strategy and exercises.
B17: Occupational safety, conventional risk, working conditions and worker dose records.
B18: Access to the environmental information, opportunity to comment before consent, and access to review procedures.

C01.n: Operating utility licensing a large reactor on a coastal site near a border
b: The Article 37 submission and the transboundary consultation have their own statutory clocks that do not wait for the safety case.
Emergency planning feasibility with a dense population nearby is decided by authorities outside the nuclear regulator.
Adapting a reference design still requires site-specific re-analysis of every external hazard.

C02.n: Developer selecting an SMR technology for an existing site with a weak grid
b: Grid weakness is a safety input, not only a commercial one, and it belongs in the design basis.
A first-of-a-kind design carries a code validation programme that is usually the longest item on the schedule.
The existing site brings inherited waste and contamination that become your problem at licensing.

C03.n: Designer developing a non-water-cooled reactor in a seismic region
b: The design guidance was written around water reactors. Every graded departure has to be argued, not assumed.
Material data at operating temperature is often the binding constraint and takes years to generate.
Analysis codes validated for water systems do not transfer, and the validation basis has to be built.

C04.n: Research reactor operator maintaining an ageing facility
b: Graded approach is a judgement that has to be re-agreed, not inherited from the original licence.
Ageing management for a facility built before modern requirements needs data that was never recorded.
Fuel return arrangements and their transport regime are a separate obligation with their own lead time.

C05.n: Licensing a dry spent fuel storage facility on an operating site
b: Criticality, shielding and heat removal are all cask questions, but the site interface is a facility question.
Storage duration assumptions drive material and ageing requirements far more than the initial design case.
The absence of a disposal route is a licensing issue even when the storage itself is sound.
Characterisation data that was never collected during operation cannot be reconstructed cheaply.
The end state has to be agreed with the regulator and the environmental authority before the work, not after.
Waste routes and acceptance criteria often do not exist for the streams you are about to create.

C07.n: Siting a deep geological disposal facility
b: The safety case runs over timescales where no standard analysis convention applies.
Public participation and access to justice are statutory, and they set the real schedule.
Transboundary consultation applies to a facility that never operates in the ordinary sense.
Criticality safety and ventilation confinement dominate, and the reactor-derived guidance does not fit.
Safeguards measures have to be built into the layout, not added to a finished plant.
Powder handling brings fire, explosion and conventional occupational risks alongside the nuclear ones.

C09.n: Long term operation and periodic safety review of an operating reactor
b: The review is against current standards, not the standards the plant was built to.
Ageing management needs a data record that starts decades before the review.
Flooding re-evaluation regularly produces modifications that were not in the plan.
The regulatory route for a factory-built, transportable unit is often unresolved in the jurisdiction.
Transport of a fuelled or irradiated unit falls under the transport regime, which was not written for it.
Emergency planning and staffing assumptions drive the concept more than the reactor physics.

C11.n: Operator arranging transport of spent fuel and waste packages
b: Package design approval and shipment approval are separate acts with separate lead times.
Route security requirements are set outside the nuclear regulator and are not public.
Transit through other states brings their approvals into your schedule.

C12.n: Designing a waste treatment and conditioning facility
b: Waste acceptance criteria come from a destination facility that may not exist yet.
Ventilation and confinement are the dominant safety systems, and reactor guidance does not cover them.
The product has to remain qualified for decades of storage, which is a materials question.

C13.n: Equipment supplier delivering a safety class item
b: Qualification is item-specific and expires. A certificate is not qualification.
The applicable code follows the safety class assigned by the designer, not from your product line.
Counterfeit and fraudulent item controls now sit in the contract and are audited.

C14.n: Releasing a remediated site from regulatory control
b: Release criteria are national and differ by an order of magnitude between neighbouring states.
Residual contamination in structures and soil is found late and changes the cost basis.
The end state agreed at the start is what determines whether the work ever finishes.

C15.n: Developer licensing a first-of-a-kind nuclear power plant in Poland
b: The Atomic Law and its implementing regulations form the licensing basis; IAEA, WENRA and vendor codes support the case but do not replace Polish legal requirements.

Site assessment, safety analyses and the preliminary safety report, and nuclear-safety design requirements are distinct statutory layers and must be checked against the current consolidated Polish texts.
Commissioning, emergency planning, waste and spent-fuel arrangements, and decommissioning funding become downstream licence obligations but need assumptions and interfaces fixed during design.

en.wb_t: First-level orientation aid — not design advice, not a determination of applicability
en.wb_s: This page maps the normative landscape of nuclear projects so that a question can be placed and asked properly. It recommends no design solution and it establishes for no document that it applies. The edition in force and the applicability to a specific project are checked separately, at the original source and with the competent authority.

en.cat_why: Why the categories are kept apart
en.cat_w1: The authority differs. A directive binds the reader; a code binds only through the route that adopts it; a utility requirement binds only through a contract; a method binds nobody.
en.cat_w2: Mixing them hides the gaps. A file that quotes industry guidance where a legal duty applies looks complete and is not.
en.cat_w3: The order below is a hierarchy of force, not of importance. A conventional standard low in the order can still be the document that decides whether an item is accepted.
en.cat_w4: Access is recorded separately from authority. A document can be mandatory and sold, or open and advisory.

en.st_bears_note: Selected mechanically: same subject area, same stage, most specific first. Not a statement that any of them requires this work.
lim: Applicability is decided by the project and by the competent authority, never by this page and never by a filter result.
Depth differs by jurisdiction and is declared. A jurisdiction marked as outlined or as framework only is not a jurisdiction with few requirements; it is one this register has not worked through.
No value, threshold, class or requirement text from a sold or access-restricted document is reproduced here. Entries name a document and describe what question it addresses.
No edition is stated anywhere on this page. Documents are revised; the edition in force is established at the source.
The register is incomplete by construction. It carries the international and European layer densely and other jurisdictions thinly.
The list of work is a prompt, not a scope of work. What a specific regulator requires is set in the national regime and in pre-application discussion.
Safety classification of an item is a design decision that the regulator will challenge. The code grid follows a class that this page cannot assign for you.
